## Production gaps

This solution runs two single-node clusters with demo credentials so that it starts in a minute. Before you reuse the design for a real migration, work through each of these topics.

### Brokers and replication

In this solution, each cluster is one broker, so every topic has replication factor 1 on both sides, and the migrator copies the source's replication factor because nothing overrides it. The `max_in_flight` setting is 29, one batch per source partition, and `sync_topic_interval` creates a topic on the target even before it carries a record.

In production, run three or more brokers on the target and set `topic_replication_factor: 3` on the `redpanda_migrator` output, so migrated topics get the target's standard even when the source used less. Set `max_in_flight` to the number of partitions you migrate, and leave `sync_topic_interval` on so that empty and low-traffic topics are created too. Run the migrator close to the target cluster: it produces every record with acknowledgments, so produce latency to the target bounds its throughput.

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/) and [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/).

### Migrator throughput

In this solution, one migrator process copies about fifty records a second across 29 partitions, and its lag stays within a few seconds of production.

In production, measure before you commit to a cutover date:

- **What to measure.** The source's produce rate per topic in records and bytes, from your existing Kafka or MSK metrics. The migrator's copy rate and `redpanda_lag` per topic and partition while it copies history, and again once it is level with live traffic. The time the initial copy of retained history takes, which is the size of the retained data divided by the copy rate you measured.
- **Tuning one process.** The `redpanda_migrator` input and output document the settings for high throughput: `partition_buffer_bytes` and `max_yield_batch_bytes` on the input, and `max_in_flight` on the output, up to the number of partitions copied in parallel. Change one at a time and measure.
- **More than one process.** The input balances the source partitions across every process that shares its `consumer_group`, so you can run more migrator processes with the same configuration. Each process also runs the topic, schema, and consumer group syncs. Alternatively, split the topics between separate migrator processes, each with one input and output pair in its own config file and its own `regexp_topics_include` pattern and consumer group, so one team's large topics do not hold up another's. Test the layout you choose on a copy of your workload, including a restart of one process mid-copy.
- **Network cost and placement.** Every record crosses the network twice: read from the source and written to the target. When the clusters are in different availability zones, regions, or clouds, both legs can be billed as cross-zone or inter-region transfer, and the initial copy moves your whole retained history. Estimate it from the retained bytes plus the produce rate times the migration window, and place the migrator where it saves the most, usually in the same zone as the target, since its writes wait for acknowledgment.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/), [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/), and [Monitoring](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/guides/monitoring/).

### Security

In this solution, both clusters run SASL/SCRAM over plaintext listeners, the application and Console sign in as the superuser, and both Schema Registries sit behind HTTP basic auth. The Kafka node's controller listener is unauthenticated and bound to the loopback interface, which is why `ANONYMOUS` is in `super.users`. The `migrator` user has the least-privilege ACLs from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/) for the one group this solution migrates, `orders-service`.

In production, enable TLS on every Kafka listener and on Schema Registry, and give each application its own credential instead of the superuser. Secure a real Kafka source's controller listeners as its operators already do; never copy this demo's single-node controller setup. Reuse the migrator's ACL set with your topic prefix or an explicit topic list, plus `DESCRIBE` on the source and `READ` on the target for every consumer group you migrate: list the same groups in `consumer_groups.include`. With `DESCRIBE` on the cluster the migrator lists every group, including ones such as Confluent Schema Registry's `schema-registry` group, and a listed group it may not describe makes the offset fetch fail for the whole sync, with `GROUP_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED` in the migrator's log. Add `sync_topic_acls` and the cluster `ALTER` it needs on the target only if ACLs migrate too. Enable Schema Registry authorization so that the registry grants are as narrow as the Kafka ones, and rotate or delete the migrator's credential on both clusters once the last group has moved.

See [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/), [Configure Authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authentication/), [Configure Access Control Lists](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authorization/acl/), [Schema Registry Authorization](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-authorization/), and the [migrator's required permissions](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/#required-permissions).

### Source authentication

In this solution, the migrator signs in to Apache Kafka with SASL/SCRAM-SHA-256 over plaintext and to Confluent Schema Registry with HTTP basic auth. That registry authenticates users from a file and authorizes nothing, so the migrator's registry user could write there.

In production, configure the `redpanda_migrator` input for your source:

- **Amazon MSK with IAM access control.** Set `sasl[].mechanism: AWS_MSK_IAM` with `sasl[].aws.region` and credentials (`from_ec2_role`, `role` to assume, or a `profile`), and turn on `tls`. Grant the IAM principal the same operations as the source ACLs in `scripts/migrator-acls.sh`, expressed as `kafka-cluster:` actions in an IAM policy: connect to and describe the cluster, read and describe the topics and their dynamic configuration, describe the groups you migrate, and describe and alter the migrator's own group. Amazon's IAM access control documentation maps each Kafka operation to its action; check the policy with the read-only proofs below.
- **Amazon MSK or Kafka with SCRAM.** Keep `SCRAM-SHA-512` or `SCRAM-SHA-256` as here, over TLS, and keep the ACLs in `scripts/migrator-acls.sh`.
- **OAUTHBEARER.** Set `sasl[].mechanism: OAUTHBEARER` with a `token`. The input sends that one token for each session and does not fetch a new one, so issue a token that outlives the migration window, or plan restarts with a fresh token, and test the behavior when it expires.
- **Confluent Schema Registry or Confluent Cloud.** The input's `schema_registry` block supports `basic_auth` (a Confluent Cloud API key and secret), `oauth`, `jwt`, and `tls` with client certificates. Give that identity read-only access to the subjects you migrate with the registry's own authorization, such as role bindings in Confluent Cloud or Confluent Platform, where it is available. Where it is not, as with the community registry here, treat the migrator's registry credential as a write credential and rotate it after the migration.

Whichever mechanism you use, run the read-only proofs from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/) against the real source before you start: listing topics works, and an idempotent produce and a `--acks 1` produce are both refused.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/) and the [migrator's required permissions](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/#required-permissions).

### Partitions

In this solution, the four topics have 12, 6, 8, and 3 partitions, and the migrator recreates each with the same count and copies every record to the same partition number.

In production, list every topic's partitions, configuration, and log start offsets with `rpk topic describe -c -p` and every subject with `rpk registry subject list` before you start; both work against Apache Kafka, Amazon MSK, and Confluent Schema Registry, so the final verification has a list to match. Keep partition counts identical during the migration: offset translation needs matching counts, and a different count on the target sends keys to other partitions. Resize on the target only after every consumer has moved. The migrator copies every topic setting on its supported list that the source reports, including Kafka's defaults such as `segment.bytes` and `max.message.bytes`, as topic-level overrides on the target, so compare `rpk topic describe -c` on both clusters and remove the overrides you want the target's cluster defaults for.

See [Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/manage-topics/).

### Schema validation

In this solution, schemas are registered on the source, the target registry stays in `IMPORT` mode until the cutover so that every ID is preserved, and no broker checks the schema ID of a record.

In production, freeze schema deletions on the source for the length of the migration, and keep `versions: all` so that consumers pinned to an old version keep working. Migrate in `IMPORT` mode with preserved IDs, return the target to `READWRITE` as the last step of the cutover, then enable schema ID validation on the migrated topics so that the target refuses a record whose schema it does not hold.

See [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/).

### Consumer scaling

In this solution, one consumer instance in `orders-service` moves by hand in [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/).

In production, list every group with `rpk group list` and `rpk group describe`, decide the order in which they move, and move each one with the same sequence: stop every instance on the source, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets, then start every instance on the target. Keep the migrator running until the last group and the last producer have moved.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Data retention

In this solution, the topics keep their source retention on the target: 7 days for `shop.orders`, compaction alone for `shop.customer-profiles`, 1 day with compaction for `shop.inventory-events`, and 1 hour for `shop.alerts`.

In production, check that the target's retention covers the migration window plus the backlog a consumer may still have at the cutover, and that the target has the disk for it.

See [Configure message retention](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/disk-utilization/#configure-message-retention).

### Compaction

In this solution, `shop.customer-profiles` is compacted and `shop.inventory-events` is compacted and deleted, but in a run this short compaction removes nothing before the migrator copies the records, so both topics hold the same number of records on the two clusters and `scripts/verify.sh` can compare the counts exactly.

In production, expect history that the source compacted before the migrator started: the source keeps the offset gaps that compaction left, and the migrator writes the remaining records one after another, so the target's high watermark for that topic is lower than the source's and the same record has different offsets. Compare compacted topics by key and latest value instead, and check each group's translated offsets by the records they point at (see [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery) for the gap case to test). Compaction runs on each cluster on its own schedule, so an older record for a key can still be on one side after it is gone from the other.

See [Compaction Settings](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/compaction-settings/).

### Cutover order

In this solution, the producer stops after the consumer has moved, the migrator drains, and `scripts/verify.sh` compares the two clusters once.

In production, create each application's user on the target and grant its ACLs there before you move it: the migrator copies no users, and copies topic ACLs only with `sync_topic_acls`, without their `WRITE` grants. Move every consumer group that reads a producer's topics before the producer, because until the producer moves, the source still has every record and each group can go back (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)). Then pause the producer, run the lag check until the migrator's lag on its topics is 0, and only then point it at the target. A producer that writes to the target before the drain finishes interleaves its records with migrated records that are still arriving, so records with the same key can land out of order. If a pause is not acceptable, accept that records produced to the target during the drain can precede migrated records with the same key. Run the comparisons in `scripts/verify.sh` as the acceptance test for each migrated topic and group, and keep the source cluster until they pass for the last one.

See [Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Rollback

In this solution, nothing is rolled back: the cutover runs forward once and `scripts/verify.sh` checks the result.

In production, plan the way back before each stage, and know which stage you are in:

- **Before any consumer moves.** The migrator only reads the source and writes the target. To abandon the migration, stop the migrator; the applications never noticed it. Delete the copied topics, schemas, and consumer groups on the target, or keep them for the next attempt.
- **After a consumer group moves, before its producers move.** The producers still write only to the source, so the source has every record and the group's committed offsets there have not moved since you stopped it. Stop the group's consumers on the target and start them on the source again with the source connection settings: they resume from the source offsets. Records the group processed on the target after the cutover are processed again, so this stage relies on the same idempotent processing as the cutover itself. The target's committed offsets for the group are now behind, and the migrator never moves a target offset backwards, so delete the group on the target (`rpk group delete`) before you try the cutover again.
- **After a producer writes to the target: the point of no return.** Records it writes exist only on the target, and the migrator copies in one direction. Going back means either copying those records to the source and then moving consumers back as above, or accepting that consumers on the source never see them. Every record the migrator copied carries its `redpanda-migrator-provenance` header and a record written to the target directly does not, so a Redpanda Connect pipeline from the target to the source can copy back only the records without that header. Build and test that pipeline before the cutover, because key order between copied-back records and the source's last records is yours to check. Decide which before you repoint the first producer, and repoint producers in the smallest groups you can, so that a rollback touches as few topics as possible.

Keep the source cluster, its consumer group offsets, and the migrator running until every group and producer has moved and `scripts/verify.sh` passes, so each earlier stage stays reversible for as long as possible.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/) and [rpk group delete](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-group/rpk-group-delete/).

### Migration runbook

In this solution, one person moves one consumer group and one producer in a few minutes.

In production, with dozens of topics and consumer groups owned by different teams, write the runbook before the migrator starts:

1. **Inventory.** List every topic with its partitions and configuration, every subject, every consumer group with its owner and the topics it reads, and every producer with the topics it writes. Note transactional producers and read_committed consumers (see [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery)).
1. **Waves.** Group the topics so that each wave holds a set of producers and every consumer group that reads their topics. A group that reads topics of two waves moves with the later one. Give each wave an owner and a window.
1. **Gate: ready to copy.** Target sized and secured, migrator ACLs or IAM policy in place for the wave's topics and groups, the read-only proofs pass on the source, target registry in `IMPORT` mode.
1. **Gate: ready to move consumers.** Migration lag within the bound you set (`scripts/lag.sh --check` with your `LAG_BOUND`) for at least a full business cycle, no movement on any `redpanda_migrator_*_errors_total` counter, and the record and schema comparisons from `scripts/verify.sh` passing for the wave's topics.
1. **Move consumers, one group at a time.** For each group: stop it, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets (`scripts/wait-for-offsets.sh`, adapted to the group), start it on the target, and check where it resumed (`scripts/resumed.sh`, adapted). No-go: any partition that resumed on another record. Rollback: move the group back to the source (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)).
1. **Gate: ready to move producers, the point of no return.** Every consumer group of the wave runs on the target, stable and caught up, and each team has signed off. Pause the producers, drain to lag 0, repoint them.
1. **Close the wave.** Run the full comparison, keep the source topics read-only until the last wave is done, then retire them, leave `IMPORT` mode after the last wave, and delete the migrator's credentials.

See [Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Idempotency and delivery

In this solution, the source's `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 trimmed records, so every copied record has a different offset on each cluster, and the consumer still resumes on the right record, which [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/) and `scripts/verify.sh` check by comparing records, not offsets. No producer is transactional and no topic has been compacted yet.

In production, plan for how the migrator translates an offset. For each committed offset, it reads the record just before it on the source and finds the first target record with that timestamp or later. For a group in the `Empty` state, it then reads that record's `redpanda-migrator-offset` header, which holds the source offset, and moves to the exact record. For a group with active members, it stops at the timestamp lookup, which can land a few records early where several records on a partition share a millisecond timestamp, so a consumer that moves while its group is still active can read those records again. The migrator never moves a target offset backwards. So:

- Stop every consumer of a group before you wait for its offsets, so the group is `Empty` and its translation is exact, and keep consumers idempotent, or deduplicating by key, across the cutover anyway.
- Repoint a producer only after the migrator's lag on its topics is 0, so that no record written directly to the target precedes a migrated record with the same key.

Three source conditions need a test of their own before the cutover, on a copy of the real topics:

- **Transactional producers and read_committed consumers.** The input here uses `transaction_isolation_level: read_committed`, so it copies only committed records and skips aborted ones, and the target never sees the transaction markers. Each commit or abort marker on the source takes an offset that has no record on the target, so offsets drift further apart. A read_committed consumer usually commits an offset just after a commit marker, and the migrator reads the record just before the committed offset to translate it. Check what happens on your topics: watch `redpanda_migrator_cg_offset_translation_errors_total` for each group, compare the records the source and target offsets point at with `scripts/compare-offsets.sh`, and move a test group before a real one. The output has no transactional setting and writes copied records outside any transaction, so a read_committed consumer on the target reads every copied record.
- **Trimmed log starts.** Retention or `DeleteRecords` moves the source's log start offset, as here. The migrator copies from the log start, so the target starts at 0. A group whose committed offset is at or below the source's log start offset is skipped (there is no earlier record to translate from), and a consumer of that group starts on the target from its `auto.offset.reset` policy. Find such groups with `rpk group describe` before the cutover.
- **Compaction gaps.** A compacted source topic has offsets with no record, and the target copy has none, so offsets differ there too. If the record just before a committed offset was compacted away, the migrator cannot read it to translate that offset. Count the translation errors per group, and compare the record each offset points at rather than the offset numbers.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/) and [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/).

### Dead-letter handling

In this solution, there is no dead-letter topic: a record the migrator cannot write is retried, and the pipeline stops on a permanent error.

In production, keep that behavior, since a migration that drops records is not a migration. Alert on `output_error` and on a rising `redpanda_lag`, fix the cause (usually a missing ACL or a full disk on the target), and keep the source until the target has been verified.

See [Error Handling](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/configuration/error_handling/).

### Observability

In this solution, `make lag` reads the migrator's Prometheus endpoint, and each cluster has its own Redpanda Console.

In production, scrape the migrator's `/metrics` (`redpanda_lag` and the `redpanda_migrator_*` counters) and both clusters into your monitoring. Alert when lag stays above a bound you set, the produce rate times the delay you accept, as `scripts/lag.sh --check` does with `LAG_BOUND`, and when any `redpanda_migrator_*_errors_total` counter moves, including `redpanda_migrator_cg_offset_translation_errors_total`.

See [Monitoring](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/guides/monitoring/) and [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/).

### Disaster recovery

In this solution, there is no standby: the source is the only other copy, and it is retired after the cutover.

In production, set up Shadowing after the migration so that a second Redpanda cluster stays level with the target, including consumer group offsets and schemas, and can take over if the target fails. The disaster recovery solution, [Survive a cluster outage without reconfiguring clients](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/), builds that setup end to end.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

In this solution, nothing reads the migrated topics except `orders-service`.

In production, enable Iceberg topics on the migrated topics that analytics needs, so the brokers write each record to an Iceberg table with no extra pipeline to run.

See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).

## The problem

A Kafka cluster carries a shop's order flow: a Go service produces, a consumer group processes every order, and Confluent Schema Registry holds the contracts. Moving to Redpanda cannot mean stopping producers, replaying history, or losing where each consumer left off.

- **One link, inside the target.** The Redpanda cluster pulls the topics, the consumer group offsets, and the schemas from Kafka itself, so there is no migration process to deploy, size, or keep running between the clusters.
- **Every record keeps its offset.** A shadow topic holds each record at the offset it has on Kafka, so a consumer moves with the offsets it already committed, untranslated.
- **Nothing writes to the target too soon.** Shadow topics refuse writes until you fail them over, so the cutover has one point of no return, and you choose when.
- **The same tool afterwards.** After the shop runs on Redpanda, the same feature keeps a standby cluster for disaster recovery.

You create one shadow link on Redpanda while the application writes to Kafka. The consumer moves first and resumes at the exact offset it stopped at, then the producer moves, and the target holds every record the source did, at the same place.

## What the system must do

- Replicate a live, SASL-secured Kafka cluster's topics, records, consumer group offsets, and Confluent Schema Registry schemas to Redpanda with one shadow link and a read-only source user
- Keep every record at its original offset and every schema at its original ID, including a schema registered mid-migration
- Measure replication lag from both clusters' high watermarks, and know why the link's own lag reading is not enough to fail over on
- Move a consumer group to Redpanda with its committed offsets untranslated, then fail over, delete the link so the target's Schema Registry takes writes, and move the producer so it carries on its numbering
- Prove the migration lost nothing, by checking the last record of every partition on both clusters

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Turn on authentication on both clusters before either accepts its first connection, and name the cluster in every command so no command can reach the wrong side. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/start-environment/))
2. Before you migrate, inventory every topic's partition count, cleanup policy, and retention and every subject's schema IDs, because those are what a migration silently breaks, and keep partition counts unchanged until every consumer has moved. (from [Seed the source cluster](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/seed-source/))
3. Migrate underneath the running application, treat each consumer group's committed offsets as its record of what it has processed, and move clients by changing only their connection settings. (from [Start the shop's workload](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/start-workload/))
4. Give the replication its own user on the source with read-only ACLs: READ and DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the migrated topics, DESCRIBE and READ on the migrated groups, and DESCRIBE on the cluster, and nothing that writes. (from [Grant the shadow link read-only access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/grant-shadow-access/))
5. Replicate topics, consumer group offsets, and schemas with one link from the target, filtered to what you migrate, and start each topic from the beginning of its log. (from [Create the shadow link](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/create-shadow-link/))
6. Measure replication lag by comparing the high watermarks each cluster reports, never from the replication's own view of the source alone, and confirm schema IDs on the target before any consumer depends on them. (from [Verify the replication](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-replication/))
7. Move each consumer group while the producer still writes to the source: stop it, wait until its committed offsets on the target equal the source's, stop syncing that group, then start it on the target. (from [Move the consumer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-consumer/))
8. Move the producer last: stop it, fail over only when the target's high watermark equals the source's on every partition, then delete the link so the target's topics and registry take writes, and start the producer there. (from [Move the producer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-producer/))
9. Accept a migration only when the two clusters agree as compared from outside: topic shapes, log start offsets, the last record of every partition by key and timestamp, schema IDs, where every consumer and producer resumed, and that forbidden requests are refused. (from [Verify the migration end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/))

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

The cluster you leave is Apache Kafka: one KRaft node (`source`) with Confluent Schema Registry (`source-registry`). The cluster you move to is a single Redpanda broker (`target`). Both run SASL/SCRAM authentication and ACLs from the first boot. The shop's application, a Go producer and the `orders-service` consumer group built on the franz-go Kafka client, works against Kafka until you move it.

- **`source` and `source-registry`**: four `shop.*` topics with different partition counts and cleanup policies, four Avro subjects, and the `orders-service` consumer group. The `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 records that retention already removed, as on a cluster that has run for months, so its offsets do not start at 0.
- **`producer`**: a Go service that writes one Avro record every 20 ms to the four topics, in the Schema Registry wire format, and stamps each record with its number in a `producer_seq` header.
- **`orders-consumer`**: the Go service `orders-service`, a consumer group on `shop.orders` that commits offsets every second.
- **The shadow link**: created on `target` with `rpk shadow create` from `config/shadow-link.yaml`. It signs in to Kafka as the `shadow` user, which has read-only ACLs, and copies the four topics with their offsets and timestamps, the committed offsets of `orders-service`, and every schema with its ID.
- **`target`**: holds the four topics as shadow topics, read-only until the cutover fails them over. Its copy of `shop.orders` starts at the same offset as Kafka's.
- **`orders-consumer-target` and `producer-target`**: the same two images, started against the target during the cutover with only their connection settings changed.
- **Redpanda Console**, one per cluster, signed in as the superuser.

### Data flow

Left to right:

1. The producer looks up the ID of each topic's schema in the Confluent Schema Registry and writes Avro records to the four `shop.*` topics on Kafka. The `orders-service` group consumes `shop.orders` and commits offsets to `__consumer_offsets`.
1. The shadow link runs inside the target broker. It signs in to Kafka as `shadow`, fetches every partition of the four topics, and writes each record at the offset it has on Kafka, with its key, headers, and timestamp.
1. The same link copies the committed offsets of `orders-service` every five seconds, as the same numbers, because the offsets mean the same records on both clusters. An offset is capped at the target partition's high watermark until the records reach the target, and it is written only while the group has no active members on the target.
1. It also polls the source registry over HTTP and imports each schema version under its source ID into the target's built-in Schema Registry.
1. At the cutover the consumer stops on Kafka, its offsets reach the target, and the same image starts on Redpanda. The producer stops, the topics fail over once both clusters hold the same records, the link is deleted, and the producer starts on Redpanda.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

A migration that cannot stop the business has four hard requirements. The applications must move without a rewrite. Every record must keep meaning the same thing, which for Avro means keeping its schema ID. Every consumer must resume at the record it would have read next. And the target must not take a write until it holds everything the source does. Redpanda meets each of these:

- **Your clients move as they are.** Redpanda speaks the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the shop's stock franz-go clients keep their consumer groups, keyed partitioning, compaction, and Avro wire format, and moving them changes `BROKERS` and `SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL` and nothing else. See [Kafka Compatibility](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/kafka-clients/).
- **Records, offsets, and schemas replicate in the broker.** Shadowing is part of Redpanda: one link copies topics with their offsets, consumer group offsets, and schemas from any Kafka API-compatible source, with nothing to run between the clusters. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).
- **Offsets need no translation.** A shadow topic keeps the source's offsets, so a committed offset names the same record on both clusters. See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).
- **Schema IDs survive.** In API mode, the link imports every version from Confluent Schema Registry under its source ID into the Schema Registry built into the broker. See [Migrate Schemas from Confluent Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/migrate-schemas-confluent/).
- **The target is read-only until you say so.** Shadow topics refuse writes until failover, so the cutover's point of no return is one command you run when the clusters agree. See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/).

## Production gaps

This solution runs two single-node clusters with demo credentials so that it starts in a minute. Before you reuse the design for a real migration, work through each topic below.

### Brokers and replication

In this solution, each cluster is one broker, so every topic has replication factor 1 on both sides, and the link copies that.

In production, run three or more brokers on the target. The link syncs `replication.factor` with each shadow topic by default, so a topic that ran with replication factor 2 on the source gets 2 on the target. Check every topic with `rpk topic describe` after the link creates it, and raise any that fall below your standard once its topic has failed over and the link no longer manages it. The link runs inside the target brokers, so size the target for the copy as well as for the applications that move to it.

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/) and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Link throughput

In this solution, one link copies about fifty records a second across 29 partitions, and the lag stays in the tens of records.

In production, measure before you commit to a cutover date:

- **What to measure.** The source's produce rate per topic in records and bytes, from your existing Kafka or MSK metrics. The link's copy rate and the lag per topic and partition while it copies history, and again once it is level with live traffic. The time the initial copy of retained history takes, which is the size of the retained data divided by the copy rate you measured.
- **Tuning the link.** The fetch settings in `client_options`, `fetch_min_bytes`, `fetch_max_bytes`, `fetch_partition_max_bytes`, and `fetch_wait_max_ms`, decide how much each fetch from the source carries and how long it waits to fill. Change one at a time and measure. The link runs inside the target brokers, so it scales with the target cluster rather than with a process you deploy.
- **Network cost and placement.** The target fetches each record from the source once, directly, so every record crosses the network between the clusters once. When the clusters are in different availability zones, regions, or clouds, that leg can be billed as cross-zone or inter-region transfer, and the initial copy moves your whole retained history. Estimate it from the retained bytes plus the produce rate times the migration window.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

### Security

In this solution, both clusters run SASL/SCRAM over plaintext listeners, the application and Console sign in as the superuser, and both Schema Registries sit behind HTTP basic auth. The Kafka node's controller listener is unauthenticated and bound to the loopback interface, which is why `ANONYMOUS` is in `super.users`. The `shadow` user has the read-only ACLs from [Grant the shadow link read-only access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/grant-shadow-access/) for the one group this solution migrates, `orders-service`.

In production, enable TLS on every Kafka listener and on Schema Registry, and give each application its own credential instead of the superuser. Secure a real Kafka source's controller listeners as its operators already do; never copy this demo's single-node controller setup. Reuse the link's ACL set with your topic prefix or an explicit topic list, plus `DESCRIBE` and `READ` for every consumer group you migrate. The link copies the source's ACLs only when `security_sync_options` lists ACL filters, and this solution sets none; if you add filters, check the target's ACLs after the link starts. The users and their passwords are not replicated: create each application's credential on the target before it moves. Delete the link's user on the source once the last group has moved.

See [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/), [Configure Authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authentication/), [Configure Access Control Lists](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authorization/acl/), and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Source authentication

In this solution, the link signs in to Apache Kafka with SASL/SCRAM-SHA-256 over plaintext and to Confluent Schema Registry with HTTP basic auth. That registry authenticates users from a file and authorizes nothing, so the link's registry user could write there.

In production, configure the link's `client_options` for your source:

- **Kafka or Confluent Platform with SCRAM.** Keep `scram_configuration` as here, over TLS (`tls_settings.enabled: true`), and keep the read-only ACLs in `scripts/shadow-acls.sh`.
- **Confluent Cloud.** Its brokers take an API key over SASL/PLAIN, so use `plain_configuration` with TLS, and give the key read access to the migrated topics and groups. Its Schema Registry takes a separate API key and secret in `auth_options.basic` of `shadow_schema_registry_api`.
- **Amazon MSK.** The link can connect only when SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 is turned on for the MSK cluster. IAM access control is not supported, and AWS Glue Schema Registry is not supported as a schema source. If your MSK cluster uses only IAM, add SCRAM for the migration or use Redpanda Migrator, which supports IAM, as the [Kafka migration solution](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) shows.
- **Mutual TLS.** Give the link a client certificate and key in `tls_settings`, to the brokers and, separately, to the registry.

Give the link's registry identity read-only access to the subjects you migrate with the registry's own authorization, such as role bindings in Confluent Cloud or Confluent Platform, where it is available. Where it is not, as with the community registry here, treat the credential as a write credential and rotate it after the migration. Whichever mechanism you use, run the read-only proof from [Grant the shadow link read-only access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/grant-shadow-access/) against the real source before you start.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Migrate Schemas from Confluent Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/migrate-schemas-confluent/).

### Partitions

In this solution, the four topics have 12, 6, 8, and 3 partitions, and the link creates each shadow topic with the same count and copies every record to the same partition and offset.

In production, list every topic's partitions, configuration, and log start offsets with `rpk topic describe -c -p` and every subject with `rpk registry subject list` before you start; both work against Apache Kafka, Amazon MSK, and Confluent Schema Registry, so the final verification has a list to match. While a topic is shadowed, change its partition count on the source only. Resize on the target after the topic has failed over and every consumer has moved.

See [Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/manage-topics/) and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Schema validation

In this solution, the link imports every schema with its source ID into the target's default context, which stays read-only until `make delete-link`, and no broker checks a record's schema ID.

In production, freeze schema deletions on the source for the length of the migration, and register any schema the moved applications need on the source before the cutover, where the link copies it. Delete the link, or pause its Schema Registry sync, right after the last failover, then enable schema ID validation on the migrated topics so that the target refuses a record whose schema it does not hold.

See [Migrate Schemas from Confluent Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/migrate-schemas-confluent/) and [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/).

### Consumer scaling

In this solution, one consumer instance in `orders-service` moves by hand in [Move the consumer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-consumer/).

In production, list every group with `rpk group list` and `rpk group describe`, include them all in the link's `group_filters`, decide the order in which they move, and move each one with the same sequence: stop every instance on the source, wait until the target holds the same committed offsets, exclude the group from the offset sync, then start every instance on the target. Keep the link until the last group and the last producer have moved.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/) and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Data retention

In this solution, the topics keep their source retention on the target, because the link syncs `retention.ms`: 7 days, 1 hour, 1 day with compaction, and compaction alone.

In production, check that the synced retention covers the migration window plus the backlog a consumer may still have at the cutover, and that the target has the disk for it, including the retained history the link copies first.

See [Configure message retention](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/disk-utilization/#configure-message-retention).

### Compaction

In this solution, `shop.customer-profiles` is compacted and `shop.inventory-events` is compacted and deleted, but in a run this short compaction removes nothing on the source.

In production, expect history that the source compacted before the link started: the source keeps the offset gaps that compaction left, and a shadow topic keeps the same gaps, because each record is written at its source offset. The high watermarks match, and a committed offset in a compacted range names the same position on both clusters. Compaction runs on each cluster on its own schedule, so an older record for a key can still be on one side after it is gone from the other: compare compacted topics by key and latest value as well as by offsets.

See [Compaction Settings](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/compaction-settings/).

### Cutover order

In this solution, one consumer group moves, the link's whole offset sync pauses, and then one producer moves after every topic fails over at once.

In production, move every consumer group that reads a producer's topics before the producer, because until the producer moves, the source still has every record and each group can go back (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)). For each group:

1. Stop its consumers on the source, and wait until the target holds the same committed offset on every partition.
1. Stop the link copying that group's offsets: add an `EXCLUDE` filter for it to `consumer_offset_sync_options.group_filters` with `rpk shadow update`, rather than pausing the whole offset sync as this solution does, so groups that have not moved yet keep being copied. The link writes a group's offsets whenever the group has no active members on the target, so without the filter a restart of the moved consumers rewinds them to the source's offsets.
1. Start its consumers on the target.

Then, for each producer, pause it, wait until the target's high watermark equals the source's on every partition of its topics, read from both clusters, and fail over those topics with `rpk shadow failover --topic`. Do not fail over on the lag `rpk shadow status` reports: it compares with the link's last view of the source, and can read 0 while the source still holds records the link has not fetched. Records produced in that window exist only on the source after the failover. Repoint the producer only after its topics report `FAILED_OVER`.

The link owns the target's Schema Registry context while it replicates schemas, even after every topic has failed over, so the target refuses new schemas until you pause the link's Schema Registry sync or delete the link. Register every schema the moved applications will need on the source before the cutover, where the link copies it, or plan to delete the link right after the last failover.

See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Rollback

In this solution, nothing is rolled back: the cutover runs forward once and `scripts/verify.sh` checks the result.

In production, plan the way back before each stage, and know which stage you are in:

- **Before any consumer moves.** The link only reads the source. To abandon the migration, delete the link with `rpk shadow delete`; the applications never noticed it. Delete the shadow topics, the copied groups, and the imported schemas on the target, or keep them for the next attempt.
- **After a consumer group moves, before its producers move.** The producers still write only to the source, so the source has every record, and the group's committed offsets there have not moved since you stopped it. Stop the group's consumers on the target and start them on the source again: they resume from the source offsets, and the records they processed on the target are processed again, so this stage relies on the same idempotent processing as the cutover itself. Because the offsets are the same numbers on both clusters, a second attempt needs no cleanup on the target: remove the group's `EXCLUDE` filter and the link copies its offsets again.
- **After a producer's topics fail over: the point of no return.** A failed-over topic cannot return to shadow mode, and records the producer writes there exist only on Redpanda. Shadowing replicates only into a Redpanda cluster, so it cannot copy them back to Kafka. Going back means copying them with another tool, such as Redpanda Migrator or MirrorMaker 2, from Redpanda to Kafka, and then moving consumers back, or accepting that consumers on the source never see them. Build and test that path before the first failover, and fail over in the smallest groups of topics you can, so that a rollback touches as few topics as possible.

Keep the source cluster and its consumer group offsets until every group and producer has moved and `scripts/verify.sh` passes, so each earlier stage stays reversible for as long as possible.

See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/) and [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Migration runbook

In this solution, one person moves one consumer group and one producer in a few minutes.

In production, with dozens of topics and consumer groups owned by different teams, write the runbook before you create the link:

1. **Inventory.** List every topic with its partitions and configuration, every subject, every consumer group with its owner and the topics it reads, and every producer with the topics it writes. Note transactional producers and read_committed consumers (see [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery)).
1. **Waves.** Group the topics so that each wave holds a set of producers and every consumer group that reads their topics. A group that reads topics of two waves moves with the later one. Give each wave an owner and a window.
1. **Gate: ready to replicate.** Target sized and secured, an Enterprise license applied, `enable_shadow_linking` on, the link's user and its read-only ACLs in place for the wave's topics and groups, and the read-only proof on the source passing. One link can carry every wave: widen its topic and group filters as waves start.
1. **Gate: ready to move consumers.** Lag measured from both clusters' high watermarks within the bound you set for at least a full business cycle, every link task `ACTIVE` in `rpk shadow status`, and the offset and schema checks from `scripts/verify.sh`, adapted to the wave's topics, passing.
1. **Move consumers, one group at a time.** For each group: stop it, wait until the target holds its committed offsets, exclude it from the offset sync, start it on the target, and check that it resumed at the same offsets (`scripts/resumed.sh`, adapted to the group). No-go: any partition that resumed elsewhere. Rollback: move the group back to the source (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)).
1. **Gate: ready to move producers, the point of no return.** Every consumer group of the wave runs on the target, stable and caught up, and each team has signed off. Pause the producers, wait until both clusters agree on every high watermark of their topics, fail those topics over, and repoint the producers.
1. **Close the wave.** Run the full comparison, and keep the source topics until the last wave is done. After the last wave, delete the link, which also returns the replicated Schema Registry context to read-write, then delete the link's user on the source.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

### Idempotency and delivery

In this solution, the source's `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 trimmed records, and every record has the same offset on both clusters, so the consumer resumes at exactly the offset it committed, which [Move the consumer](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration-shadowing/move-consumer/) and `scripts/verify.sh` check. No producer is transactional.

In production, the offsets need no translation: a shadow topic writes each record at its source offset, so trimmed log starts, compaction gaps, and active groups do not move a consumer's position, as they can with a tool that copies records to new offsets. A consumer still reads again any record it processed after its last commit on the source, so keep consumers idempotent, or deduplicating by key, across the cutover. And fail over a producer's topics only when both clusters report the same high watermark on every partition, so no record is left behind on the source.

Test transactional producers and read_committed consumers on a copy of the real topics before the cutover: produce transactions on the source, abort some, and check that a read_committed consumer on the target reads the same committed records and none of the aborted ones.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/) and [Transactions](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/transactions/).

### Dead-letter handling

In this solution, there is no dead-letter topic, and none is needed: the link copies records as they are, and a task that fails reports a state other than `ACTIVE` in `rpk shadow status`.

In production, keep it that way, since a migration that drops records is not a migration. Alert when a task leaves `ACTIVE` or when lag measured from both clusters keeps rising, fix the cause, usually a missing ACL on the source or a full disk on the target, and keep the source until the target has been verified.

See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/).

### Observability

In this solution, `make lag` compares both clusters' high watermarks, `rpk shadow status` shows the link's tasks, and each cluster has its own Redpanda Console.

In production, scrape both clusters into your monitoring and chart the difference between the source's and the target's high watermarks per topic. Alert when it stays above a bound you set, the produce rate times the delay you accept, and when any task in `rpk shadow status` leaves `ACTIVE`. Use the link's own lag reading for trends, not for the cutover: it compares with the link's last view of the source, which it refreshes periodically.

See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/) and [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/).

### Disaster recovery

In this solution, there is no standby: the source is the only other copy, and it is retired after the cutover.

In production, set up Shadowing after the migration so that a second Redpanda cluster stays level with the target, including consumer group offsets and schemas, and can take over if the target fails. The disaster recovery solution, [Survive a cluster outage without reconfiguring clients](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/), builds that setup end to end.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

In this solution, nothing reads the migrated topics except `orders-service`.

In production, enable Iceberg topics on the migrated topics that analytics needs, so the brokers write each record to an Iceberg table with no extra pipeline to run.

See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).

# Agent companion: Keep a live leaderboard current as game events stream in

Generated from the multiplayer-gaming solution (v1.0.0). Human guide: https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/

## The problem

A studio runs a competitive arena mode with tens of thousands of concurrent matches and a few thousand player events a second at peak. The leaderboard and the analytics team share one Postgres, so match-night reports stall the board, achievements arrive minutes late from a batch job, and a scoring bug cannot be replayed.

You build the leaderboard, the match history, and the achievements feed on one Redpanda event stream, each in its own consumer group, at laptop scale: 24 simulated players at 100 events a second, with bursts of up to 2000 a second. You finish with a live dashboard, a match history in Postgres, and an achievements feed, proven by one script.

- **The board never waits on reporting.** The leaderboard, match history, and achievements each read the same stream in their own consumer group, so a slow or stalled database sink cannot hold the board back.
- **A scoring bug is a replay, not a data patch.** A corrected rule replays the season's events into a new board next to the live one, with no downtime and nothing rewritten in place.
- **Progress survives a deploy.** Each player's achievement progress is saved to a compacted topic and restored when an instance takes over the player's partition, so a restart never resets a streak.
- **The next feature is a consumer group, not an integration.** Anti-cheat, live-ops dashboards, and personalization read the same stream without a change to the game servers.

## What the system must do

- Publish Protobuf events under a Schema Registry contract with `BACKWARD` compatibility, register a compatible second version, and watch Schema Registry refuse a breaking change
- Materialize a live view in a compacted topic by publishing state instead of deltas
- Land a stream in Postgres with Redpanda Connect and route every bad record to a dead-letter topic
- Keep stateful, per-player logic correct across a restart by keying on the player and saving the state to a compacted topic
- Fan one topic out to three consumer groups that scale, fail, and restart independently, and replay a scoring fix into a new topic next to the live view

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Start every service before its topic and schema exist, and have it poll and log what it is waiting for, instead of exiting or creating what is missing. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/start-environment/))
2. Key every event by the entity a consumer keeps state for, and give each topic at least as many partitions as the largest consumer group will run instances. (from [Create the topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/create-topics/))
3. Register each topic's schema under the `<topic>-value` subject with `BACKWARD` compatibility before anything produces, and make producers look the schema up and wait for it, never register it. (from [Register the schemas](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/register-schemas/))
4. Produce with idempotence on, `acks=all`, and a partitioner that hashes keys the way the Java client does, so a retry is never applied twice and one key reaches one partition from any client. (from [Produce the player events](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/produce-player-events/))
5. Publish absolute state, never deltas, to a compacted topic keyed by the entity, record in each entry the source offset it was computed from, and commit input offsets only after the output is acknowledged. (from [Build the live leaderboard](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/build-leaderboard/))
6. Give each sink its own consumer group, and route every record it cannot process to a dead-letter topic with the error attached instead of stopping or dropping it. (from [Persist the match history](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/persist-match-history/))
7. Keep per-entity state in the consumer only when the input topic is keyed by that entity, save it to a compacted topic with the source offset it covers, load it when a partition is assigned, and judge time by the event's timestamp, not the wall clock. (from [Detect the achievements](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/detect-achievements/))
8. Treat the source topic as the truth: retain it for the replay window you need, add consumer instances when lag keeps growing (never more than the partition count), and rebuild a view by replaying into a new topic in a new group, then switching readers to it. (from [Scale, restart, and replay the consumers](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/scale-and-replay/))
9. Prove the system by checking that independent consumers of one stream agree with each other, using numbers observable from outside the services: high watermarks, group lag, and sink counts. (from [Verify the system end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/verify-end-to-end/))

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

A game simulator produces `GameEvent` records to two topics. Three consumers read them: a Go leaderboard service that totals each player's score and publishes it to a compacted topic that a small dashboard reads, a Redpanda Connect pipeline that writes match history to Postgres, and a Go achievements service that detects streaks and wins and publishes them back to Redpanda. Redpanda Console shows every schema-backed record decoded.

- **Game simulator** (Go, franz-go): deterministic event stream, idempotent producer, admin API to burst load or inject a poison record.
- **`game.player-events`** and **`game.match-events`**: the two source topics, keyed by `player_id` and `match_id`.
- **Schema Registry**: holds the `GameEvent` Protobuf schema as subjects `<topic>-value` with `BACKWARD` compatibility.
- **Leaderboard service** (Go): consumer group `leaderboard`, one in-memory total per player, publishes the absolute total to `game.leaderboard` after every score change, scales to three instances.
- **`game.leaderboard`**: a compacted topic keyed by `player_id`. Compaction keeps the newest total per player, so the topic is the leaderboard.
- **Leaderboard dashboard** (Go): reads `game.leaderboard` from the start with no consumer group and serves the live top 10 over server-sent events on a fixed port.
- **Redpanda Connect**: consumer group `connect-history`, decodes with Schema Registry, flattens the `oneof`, inserts into Postgres, routes failures to `game.player-events.dlq`.
- **Achievements service** (Go): consumer group `achievements`, per-player state kept in memory because every player lives on one partition and saved to the compacted topic `game.achievements.state` so a restart picks it up, produces to `game.achievements`.
- **Redpanda Console**: decodes Protobuf records with the same schemas.

### Data flow

Left to right:

1. The simulator looks the `GameEvent` schema up in Schema Registry (it never registers one; the contract is created in [Register the schemas](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/register-schemas/)) and produces every event about a player to `game.player-events`, keyed by `player_id`, and every match lifecycle event to `game.match-events`, keyed by `match_id`.
1. Three consumer groups read `game.player-events`.
1. The `leaderboard` group adds each `score_changed` delta to the player's total and publishes that total to `game.leaderboard`, a compacted topic keyed by `player_id`. The dashboard reads that topic from the start and serves the top 10.
1. The `connect-history` group, a Redpanda Connect pipeline, decodes each record through Schema Registry, flattens it, and inserts it into Postgres. A record it cannot decode goes to `game.player-events.dlq` with the error attached.
1. The `achievements` group folds each player's events into a small in-memory state, produces `achievement_unlocked` events to `game.achievements`, and saves the state to `game.achievements.state`, a compacted topic it reads back whenever it is assigned partitions.
1. The dashed `leaderboard-v2` service runs only in [Scale, restart, and replay the consumers](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/scale-and-replay/): the leaderboard image with a corrected scoring rule, in its own group, replaying `game.player-events` from the first record into `game.leaderboard.v2` while the live board stays untouched.
1. Console decodes the Protobuf topics with the same schemas; the state topic holds plain JSON. On the dead-letter topic it decodes whatever still carries a registered schema ID and shows the raw bytes and the `error` header for anything else, which is what you want when you inspect a poison record.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

A live leaderboard puts four demands on the system that carries game events. Match traffic arrives in bursts, and the board has to keep up with them. Each player's events have to be applied in order. The leaderboard, the achievements service, and match history read the same events at their own pace, and a scoring bug has to be fixable by replaying the season. And a small studio team has to run all of it. Redpanda meets each of these:

- **Built for bursts.** Redpanda is written in C++ and designed for high throughput with low tail latency on modest hardware, so a burst of match events is appended and fanned out without a bigger cluster to absorb it. See [Redpanda differentiators](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/get-started/intro-to-events/#redpanda-differentiators).
- **One binary to run.** The broker and [Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/) are one binary with no external dependencies, so the whole broker side here is one container, and Console and Redpanda Connect decode Protobuf records with no extra service to run.
- **A contract between teams, enforced in one place.** The game client and the backend services share Protobuf schemas through that built-in registry, which refuses an incompatible change before any consumer sees it, as [Register the schemas](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/register-schemas/) shows.
- **Replay without a second system.** Each consumer group keeps its own [committed offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/), so [Scale, restart, and replay the consumers](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/multiplayer-gaming/scale-and-replay/) rebuilds the leaderboard into a new topic while the live board keeps serving. The optional Tiered Storage extension on the last step moves old segments of `game.player-events` to object storage, so how far back a replay reaches is a retention setting instead of a disk size. See [Use Tiered Storage](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/tiered-storage/).
- **Sinks without code.** Redpanda Connect decodes, flattens, and [inserts](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/sql_insert/) match history into Postgres, with a dead-letter topic, from one YAML file.

Redpanda speaks the Kafka API, so the Go services are ordinary Kafka clients ([franz-go](https://github.com/twmb/franz-go)) and the partitioning, consumer group, and compaction behavior your team already knows applies unchanged. If you run Kafka or MSK today, [the Kafka migration solution](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) moves a live workload's topics, schemas, and consumer group offsets to Redpanda.

## The problem

A retailer runs two storefronts after an acquisition: one brand's orders are in Postgres, the other's in MySQL. Finance reconciles them from a day-old export, and support needs one view of all orders within a minute to tell a customer whether a cancellation went through. The usual fix is a change data capture (CDC) connector on Kafka Connect and a sink connector into the lakehouse.

You build it with two moving parts: Redpanda Connect streams both databases' changes into one topic, and Redpanda writes that topic as an Iceberg table that Spark queries. At the end, one Spark view shows the current orders from both storefronts within seconds of each change.

## What the system must do

- Capture inserts, updates, and deletes from Postgres and MySQL with the Redpanda Connect `postgres_cdc` and `mysql_cdc` inputs, without Debezium or a Kafka Connect cluster
- Shape a raw change event into a lakehouse row with one Bloblang mapping, and give the Iceberg table its columns by registering a schema
- Make every change queryable in the lakehouse seconds after it happens, by setting one topic property that makes Redpanda write `cdc_orders` as an Iceberg table itself
- Query the change log in Spark SQL and define a view that gives analysts the current state of both source tables
- Prove that every change the databases made reached the topic and the Iceberg table, and that the current-state view matches each database row for row

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Capture from a real database with logical write-ahead logging or row-based binary logging and a replica identity set before the first change, and write Iceberg tables through the cluster's existing Tiered Storage bucket rather than a separate sink. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/start-environment/))
2. Turn Iceberg on for a topic before anything produces to it, because translation starts where the property was set, and use `value_schema_latest` only when every producer writes one shape you keep in step with the registered schema. (from [Turn the topic into a lakehouse table](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/enable-iceberg-topics/))
3. Snapshot the table before streaming its change log, give the capture a named replication slot so a restart resumes instead of snapshotting again, and alert on the slot, because the database cannot reclaim log the slot has not acknowledged. (from [Capture Postgres changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-postgres-changes/))
4. Flatten each change into one row before it reaches the lakehouse, with the operation as a word, a literal source, the database's log position, a capture timestamp, and money as exact decimal text, never floating point, and log full rows for tables whose deleted values you need. (from [Shape the change events](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/shape-events/))
5. Keep the lakehouse table an append-only change log and give analysts current state through one shared view: take the newest change per row and drop rows whose newest change is a delete, which also collapses at-least-once duplicates. (from [Query the lakehouse with Spark](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/query-with-spark/))
6. Write the changes from every source database into one table with a literal `source` column, and reconstruct rows by source and primary key together, because separate databases reuse the same ids. (from [Capture MySQL changes](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/capture-mysql-changes/))
7. Prove the pipeline with two invariants, the topic's high watermarks equal the lakehouse table's row count and the current-state view holds exactly the rows and values each source holds now, because the quiet failures leave every service healthy and only the data disagrees. (from [Verify the pipeline end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/))

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

Two operational databases, one streaming pipeline each, and one lakehouse table. Redpanda Connect follows each database's change log and writes a flat event per row change to the `cdc_orders` topic. Because that topic has `redpanda.iceberg.mode` set, the brokers write the topic's records into RustFS as an Iceberg table and commit each new snapshot to an Iceberg REST catalog. Spark reads the table through the same catalog, and Redpanda Console shows the topic and its schema.

- **Postgres** with a `pandashop` database and an `orders` table of five rows: the first storefront's database, with `wal_level=logical` so its write-ahead log can be decoded.
- **MySQL** 8.4 with the same table and two rows: the second storefront's database, with row-based binary logging. Its order ids also start at 1, so every event carries a `source` column that tells the two apart.
- **Redpanda Connect**, twice: one pipeline per database, each with a CDC input, a Bloblang mapping, and a `redpanda` output. Both write to the same topic, and the MySQL pipeline keeps its binary log position in a compacted `cdc_checkpoints` topic.
- **Redpanda** with Tiered Storage, Iceberg topics, and its built-in Schema Registry. It is the broker, and it also writes the table's files and commits its snapshots.
- **RustFS** as the S3-compatible object store, holding both the Tiered Storage segments and the Iceberg table files.
- **An Iceberg REST catalog** (`apache/iceberg-rest-fixture`), which Redpanda commits table snapshots to and Spark discovers tables through.
- **Apache Spark** as the query engine, running `spark-sql` against the catalog.
- **Redpanda Console**, to inspect the topic, its configuration, and the registered schema.

### Data flow

Left to right: an application changes a row in Postgres. Postgres writes that change to its write-ahead log. Redpanda Connect holds a logical replication slot on that log, decodes the change, and the pipeline's Bloblang mapping turns it into one flat event with the operation, the row's values, the change log position, and a capture timestamp. The `redpanda` output writes the event to `cdc_orders`, keyed by `order_id`, one batch at a time with idempotent writes, so every change to one order lands in one partition in the order the database applied them.

From there Redpanda does the work a sink connector would normally do. The topic's `redpanda.iceberg.mode` is `value_schema_latest`, so the brokers read the latest schema registered for the `cdc_orders-value` subject, use it to lay out an Iceberg table, deserialize each record against it, and write Parquet data files into the same RustFS bucket Tiered Storage uses. They commit a new table snapshot to the REST catalog within the lag target: this solution sets 10 seconds, and the default is one minute. A record the schema cannot deserialize goes to a separate `cdc_orders~dlq` table rather than being dropped.

Spark asks the catalog for the table, reads the Parquet files straight out of RustFS, and sees the change log as rows. The MySQL pipeline is the same shape with a different input, and it writes to the same topic, so one table answers questions about both storefronts.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

Getting database changes into a lakehouse usually takes three systems between the database and the table: a change capture service on a Kafka Connect cluster, a Kafka cluster, and a sink connector that writes Iceberg files and commits them to a catalog. Each one is another thing to deploy, size, secure, and debug when a change fails to appear. This solution needs only two moving parts between the databases and the table, Redpanda Connect and the broker, and Redpanda is what makes that possible:

- **The broker writes and commits the Iceberg table.** One topic property turns a topic into an Iceberg table, so there is no sink connector to deploy and no second copy of the data: the Parquet files and the topic's Tiered Storage segments live in the same bucket. You still own table maintenance, such as compacting small files, and the current-state view analysts query; [analytics and lakehouse](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-analytics-and-lakehouse) says who runs what. See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).
- **The table's columns come from the built-in Schema Registry.** Redpanda lays the table out from the latest schema registered for the topic's subject, in the same binary as the broker, so the schema that validates the change events is the one that shapes the table. See [Specify Iceberg Schema](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/specify-iceberg-schema/).
- **CDC is a pipeline, not a cluster.** The Redpanda Connect `postgres_cdc` and `mysql_cdc` inputs read the write-ahead log and the binary log from one process each, with no Kafka Connect cluster. See [postgres_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/postgres_cdc/) and [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/).
- **Tiered Storage is the object store wiring.** Iceberg topics write through the cluster's Tiered Storage configuration: one bucket and one set of credentials. See [Use Tiered Storage](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/tiered-storage/).

The change topic is still an ordinary Kafka topic. Keyed partitioning keeps each order's changes in order, and any Kafka client can read the stream in its own consumer group while Redpanda writes the table. If you run Kafka or Amazon MSK today, the [Kafka migration solution](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) moves a live workload's topics, schemas, and consumer group offsets to Redpanda.
