## Production gaps

This solution runs one broker, one RustFS container, and two single-node databases with no authentication, so that it starts in a few minutes. Before you build a pipeline like this against production databases, work through each topic in this section.

### Brokers and replication

This solution runs one broker in `dev-container` mode with `--memory 1G` and replication factor 1. Iceberg translation runs on the partition leader, so it shares the broker's one core with everything else the broker does.

Run three or more brokers with replication factor 3, for `cdc_orders` and the `cdc_checkpoints` topic alike. Size the cluster for Iceberg translation rather than assuming spare capacity: each translating partition adds CPU on its leader and requests to the object store. Iceberg topics and Tiered Storage are Enterprise features: this stack runs them on the 30-day trial a new cluster starts with, and a production cluster needs a Redpanda Enterprise license, in addition to the license the CDC inputs need in Redpanda Connect.

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/), [Tune Performance for Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-performance-tuning/), and [Redpanda Licenses and Enterprise Features](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/get-started/licensing/overview/).

### Security

This solution uses plaintext everywhere. The broker and the catalog accept unauthenticated connections, and the databases and RustFS use fixed local credentials from `.env`.

Enable TLS and SASL on the broker. Give each change data capture (CDC) pipeline a database account whose only privileges are the ones capture needs: replication and `SELECT` on the captured tables, plus `RELOAD` for the MySQL snapshot's read lock. Use IAM roles or scoped keys for the object store, and authenticate the REST catalog with `oauth2`, `bearer`, or `aws_sigv4`. Keep the CDC credentials out of the pipeline file: read them from a secrets store.

See [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/) and [Use Iceberg Catalogs](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/use-iceberg-catalogs/).

### Source database and capture

This solution sets `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` on the Postgres `orders` table and runs MySQL with `binlog_row_image=FULL`, so a delete event carries the values the row held. Postgres keeps the pipeline's position in the named replication slot `cdc_to_lakehouse_orders`. The MySQL snapshot takes `FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK` on a two-row table, which is over before you notice it.

Decide the replica identity and the binary log row image per table, because each one adds the full old row to the log for every update and delete. Alert on the replication slot's retained log in Postgres: the database cannot reclaim log a slot has not acknowledged, so a stopped pipeline fills the disk. If you cap it with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, Postgres invalidates a slot that falls behind the cap, and the pipeline can only start over with a snapshot, which cannot report the rows deleted in the meantime: those rows stay live in the lakehouse as ghost rows. Keep the MySQL binary log for longer than the longest pipeline outage you plan to recover from, for the same reason. Schedule the first MySQL snapshot of a large table in a maintenance window, because the read lock it takes is global. When you change a captured table's columns, change the schema and the mapping with it, as the schema drift extension on the last step shows: an added column is silently left out, and a changed type sends every change to the dead-letter table.

See [postgres_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/postgres_cdc/) and [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/).

### Backfill and re-snapshot

This solution snapshots each table once, on a fresh stack, into an empty topic. A pipeline has to snapshot again whenever it has lost its place: the Postgres replication slot was dropped or invalidated by `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, the MySQL checkpoint is gone or points at a binary log file MySQL has already purged, or a snapshot was interrupted before it finished. A snapshot reads the rows that exist, so a row deleted while the pipeline had no position never gets a delete event, and the current-state view keeps it as a live ghost row forever.

Treat a re-snapshot as a reload, not a catch-up:

1. Stop the pipeline and drop its position: the replication slot in Postgres, or, for MySQL, the pipeline's `checkpoint_key` in `cdc_checkpoints`, by producing a tombstone for that key with `rpk topic produce -Z`.
1. Create a new topic, such as `cdc_orders_v2`, with the same Iceberg settings and schema subject, and point the pipeline's output at it. Redpanda writes it as a new table.
1. Start the pipeline. It snapshots into the new topic and streams from the new position.
1. When the new table has caught up, repoint `orders_current` at it, and delete the old topic, which also drops its table while `redpanda.iceberg.delete` is `true`.

Analysts keep reading the view throughout, and the old table stays correct until you switch. For a large table, raise `snapshot_batch_size` (Postgres) or `snapshot_max_batch_size` (MySQL), raise `max_parallel_snapshot_tables` when Postgres snapshots many tables, size the topic's partitions for the snapshot burst, and schedule the MySQL snapshot in a maintenance window, because it takes a global read lock to fix its starting position. Prevent the need where you can: alert on slot lag before `max_slot_wal_keep_size` invalidates the slot, and keep the MySQL binary log longer than the longest outage you plan to recover from.

See [postgres_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/postgres_cdc/) and [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/).

### Partitions

This solution gives `cdc_orders` one partition, keyed by `order_id`. Every change to one order stays in order because it lands in that one partition, with the pipeline settings [Shape the change events](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/shape-events/) lists keeping the batches in order.

Size partitions for the change rate before the first change arrives, and keep the key. Ordering per row holds only within a partition, and an update that overtakes its insert produces a table that reconstructs to the wrong state. Adding partitions later moves keys to other partitions, so a row's next change can get a lower offset than its last one in the old partition; rebuild into a new topic, as [backfill and re-snapshot](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-backfill-and-resnapshot) describes, rather than adding partitions to a live CDC topic.

See [Sizing Guidelines](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/sizing/).

### Schema validation

This solution registers a JSON schema for `cdc_orders-value`, and Redpanda uses it to lay out the table in `value_schema_latest` mode. Nothing stops a producer writing a record that does not match it: the record goes to the dead-letter table instead.

Once more than one pipeline or schema version writes the topic, encode records in the Schema Registry wire format with the Redpanda Connect `schema_registry_encode` processor, switch the topic to `value_schema_id_prefix`, and enable schema ID validation, so a record without a registered schema is rejected at produce time. Register a schema change before the pipeline that writes it: Redpanda caches the latest schema for `iceberg_latest_schema_cache_ttl_ms`, five minutes by default.

See [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/) and [Specify Iceberg Schema](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/specify-iceberg-schema/).

### Iceberg commit timing

This solution sets `iceberg_target_lag_ms` and `iceberg_catalog_commit_interval_ms` to 10 seconds, the lowest commit interval Redpanda accepts, so a change is queryable in the lakehouse within seconds. Both default to one minute.

Start from the defaults. A tighter lag trades query freshness for many small Parquet files and more catalog commits, and small files make every query engine slower until something compacts them, which Redpanda does not do (see [analytics and lakehouse](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-analytics-and-lakehouse)). Lower the lag only for the topics whose readers need it, and watch translation lag and file counts when you do.

See [Tune Performance for Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-performance-tuning/).

### Consumer scaling

Nothing in this solution consumes `cdc_orders` through the Kafka API: the lakehouse write is the broker's own work, and Spark reads object storage.

Iceberg translation costs no consumer group, and the topic still serves streaming readers. Applications that need the changes as a stream read it in their own consumer groups without affecting the table.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Data retention

This solution leaves default retention on a one-partition topic, with Tiered Storage writes on.

The Iceberg table outlives the topic's retention: data written to Iceberg stays queryable after the records age out of the topic. Set the topic's retention for the streaming consumers, and keep the table as the history. Deleting the topic drops its table while `redpanda.iceberg.delete` is `true`, which is the default, so set it to `false` on any topic whose table must survive the topic.

See [Use Tiered Storage](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/tiered-storage/) and [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).

### Idempotency and delivery

The pipelines' `redpanda` output batches 50 events or one second, sends one batch at a time (`max_in_flight: 1`), and writes idempotently (`idempotent_write: true`, with `acks` at `all`), and each pipeline runs one processing thread. Those settings keep a producer retry from duplicating or reordering a batch, which the current-state view depends on, because it orders changes by offset. They do not make the pipeline exactly-once: on a restart, `postgres_cdc` resumes from the replication slot's position and `mysql_cdc` from its checkpoint, so changes delivered after the last acknowledged position are written again, in their original order.

CDC is at-least-once, so the table is an append-only log that can hold duplicates. Deduplicate in the query, as the [`orders_current` view](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/query-with-spark/) already does by taking the newest change per row, or on the way in, and make every reader tolerate a repeat. Keep the ordering settings when you tune for throughput: more pipeline threads or batches in flight let changes to one row reach the topic out of order.

See [Idempotent producers](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/produce-data/idempotent-producers/).

### State and checkpoints

In this solution, Postgres holds the `postgres_cdc` position in the replication slot on the database server. MySQL has no server-side cursor, so `mysql_cdc` keeps its binary log position in the `binlog_position` cache resource, a `redpanda` cache that writes it to the compacted `cdc_checkpoints` topic, so a restart resumes from the last acknowledged position.

A lost position is worse than a slow restart. With a `memory` cache, a restarted MySQL pipeline has no position, so it takes a fresh snapshot under a global read lock and writes every row again. A Postgres slot invalidated by `max_slot_wal_keep_size` forces the same. A snapshot cannot emit deletes, so any row deleted while the position was lost has no delete event, and the current-state view shows it as live forever.

Keep the checkpoint topic replicated like any other topic, with a `checkpoint_key` per pipeline, or use another durable cache, such as `redis` or `aws_dynamodb`. Alert on the slot's retained log before it reaches `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, and on MySQL binary log retention shorter than your longest outage. When a position is lost anyway, rebuild as [backfill and re-snapshot](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/cdc-to-lakehouse/verify-end-to-end/#prod-backfill-and-resnapshot) describes instead of snapshotting into the existing table.

See [mysql_cdc](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/mysql_cdc/), [redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/caches/redpanda/), and [Caches](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/caches/about/).

### Dead-letter handling

This solution leaves `redpanda.iceberg.invalid.record.action` at `dlq_table`, the default, so a record the schema cannot deserialize goes to a `cdc_orders~dlq` table. The verify script checks that the table does not exist.

Alert on the `redpanda_iceberg_translation_dlq_files_created` metric, query the dead-letter table when it moves, and decide per topic whether an invalid record should be kept for inspection or dropped.

See [Troubleshoot Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-troubleshooting/).

### Observability

This solution checks the pipeline by hand: `rpk topic describe`, `make dlq`, a Spark query, and the verify script.

Turn those checks into monitors. Alert on Iceberg translation lag and the dead-letter metric, on the replication slot's size in Postgres (an unconsumed slot fills the disk), and on the Redpanda Connect pipelines' own output metrics. Reconcile each source table against the current-state view periodically, as the verify script does row by row, or with counts and per-column checksums on a large table, because the quiet failures leave every service healthy and only the data disagrees.

See [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/) and [Troubleshoot Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-troubleshooting/).

### Disaster recovery

This solution has no recovery path: one broker and one bucket, and the Iceberg files are the only copy of the table.

The table's files live in object storage, with that store's own durability, and the topic can be shadowed to a second cluster. Choose which of the two you recover from: the topic replays, but the second cluster writes its own Iceberg table.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

This solution runs one Spark container that reads the table through the test REST catalog, and an `orders_current` view over the change log. Nothing compacts the table, which is fine for a few dozen rows.

The broker writes the Parquet files, commits each snapshot to the catalog, and expires old snapshots on its own schedule, five days by default, which also bounds time travel. The rest of the table's upkeep is yours:

- Compact small files. Every translation interval writes new Parquet files, so a busy or low-lag topic accumulates many small ones, and every query engine slows down reading them. AWS Glue and Databricks compact Iceberg tables automatically; otherwise schedule a Spark compaction job, such as the Iceberg `rewrite_data_files` procedure.
- Remove orphan files, such as data files from failed writes, with the Iceberg `remove_orphan_files` procedure, if your catalog does not.
- Own current state. Keep the view as the definition of current state, and once the change log is large, add a scheduled `MERGE INTO` a current-state table that the view's logic defines, so readers stop scanning every change.

Choose the catalog for the platform the analysts already use. AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Open Catalog, and GCP Lakehouse are supported integrations. Glue must be in the same AWS account and region as the cluster. Unity Catalog compacts through predictive optimization, which you enable in the workspace, and the cluster needs `iceberg_disable_snapshot_tagging` set to write to it. Apache Polaris and other REST catalogs have been tested but are not regularly verified. Give each cluster its own namespace if more than one cluster writes to the catalog.

See [Tune Performance for Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/iceberg-performance-tuning/), [Use Iceberg Catalogs](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/use-iceberg-catalogs/), and [Query Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/query-iceberg-topics/).

### Kubernetes

This solution runs on Docker Compose, or on Kubernetes with the Redpanda Operator through `make k8s-up`, with RustFS and the catalog as one service each. RustFS is here for development and evaluation only: it is not a supported object store for production Tiered Storage.

Deploy Redpanda with the Redpanda Operator, as `kubernetes/redpanda.yaml` does, and point it at a supported object store (Amazon S3, Azure ADLS, or Google Cloud Storage) and your own Iceberg catalog instead of RustFS and the test catalog.

See [Deploy Redpanda for Production in Kubernetes](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/kubernetes/k-production-deployment/) and [Use Iceberg Catalogs](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/use-iceberg-catalogs/).

## The problem

A Kafka cluster carries a shop's order flow: a Go service produces, a consumer group processes every order, and Schema Registry holds the contracts. Moving to Redpanda cannot mean stopping producers, replaying history, or losing where each consumer left off.

Redpanda Migrator copies topics, records, schemas, and offsets while the application writes. The consumer moves by changing two connection settings and resumes on the record it would have read next, although that record's offset differs on Redpanda.

**Note:** [Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/) is the recommended way to migrate from Kafka to Redpanda: a shadow link inside the target keeps every record at its source offset, so consumers move with their committed offsets untranslated. Use this Redpanda Migrator solution only when Shadowing cannot migrate your workload: the cluster you migrate to cannot run Shadowing (a version before 25.3, or no Enterprise Edition license), the source accepts only IAM or OAUTHBEARER authentication, your rollback plan needs records copied back to Kafka, or records must be renamed, filtered, or transformed on the way.

## What the system must do

- Move a live, SASL-secured cluster's topics, records, schemas, and consumer group offsets to Redpanda continuously, with a migration user that holds least-privilege ACLs on both clusters
- Keep schema IDs identical so that records already on the wire decode on the new cluster, including schemas registered mid-migration
- Read migration lag from the migrator's metrics and know when the target has caught up
- Cut a consumer group over to Redpanda from translated offsets by changing only its connection settings, then return the target Schema Registry to normal operation
- Prove the migration with exact assertions: partitions, configurations, record counts, schema IDs, and the record each consumer resumes on

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Turn on authentication on both clusters before either accepts its first connection, and name the cluster in every command so no command can reach the wrong side. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/start-environment/))
2. Before you migrate, inventory every topic's partition count, cleanup policy, and retention and every subject's schema IDs, because those are what a migration silently breaks, and keep partition counts unchanged until every consumer has moved. (from [Seed the source cluster](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/seed-source/))
3. Migrate underneath the running application, treat each consumer group's committed offsets as its record of what it has processed, and move clients by changing only their connection settings. (from [Start the shop's workload](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/start-workload/))
4. Run the migration tool as its own user with read-only ACLs on the source and prefixed create and write ACLs on the target, including `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` on source topics and `READ` on target topics, and put the target Schema Registry in `IMPORT` mode before any schema reaches it. (from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/))
5. Move records, topic configurations, schemas, and consumer group offsets with one pipeline while the application keeps writing, keep schema IDs untranslated, and sync group offsets often enough that the cutover waits seconds. (from [Start the migration](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/start-migrator/))
6. Preserve every schema's ID and version on the target and sync the registry more often than schemas change, so copied records decode there and a schema registered mid-migration arrives before a record that uses it. (from [Verify the schemas](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-schemas/))
7. Gate the cutover on observable conditions, migration lag within a stated bound while traffic runs and at zero before a producer moves, and translated offsets that point at the same records as the source's, and watch the error counters as the audit trail. (from [Monitor the migration lag](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/monitor-lag/))
8. Cut over one consumer group at a time: stop the consumer, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets, and start it on the target; then pause the producer, drain to lag 0, and repoint it, which is the point of no return, and switch the target registry to `READWRITE` only after that. (from [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/))
9. Accept a migration only when the two clusters agree as compared from outside, on topic shapes, record counts, schema IDs, the records each consumer group resumes on, and security posture, including checks that forbidden requests are refused, and never on offset numbers being equal. (from [Verify end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/))

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

The cluster you leave is Apache Kafka: one KRaft node (`source`) with Confluent Schema Registry (`source-registry`). The cluster you move to is a single Redpanda broker (`target`). Both run SASL/SCRAM authentication and ACLs from the first boot. The shop's application, a Go producer and the `orders-service` consumer group built on the franz-go Kafka client, works against Kafka the whole time. Redpanda Migrator copies everything to Redpanda, and at the end you move the consumer.

- **`source` and `source-registry`**: four `shop.*` topics with different partition counts and cleanup policies, four Avro subjects, and the `orders-service` consumer group. The `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 records that retention already removed, as on a cluster that has run for months, so its offsets do not start at 0.
- **`producer`**: a Go service that writes one Avro record every 20 ms to the four topics, in the Schema Registry wire format with the IDs from the source registry.
- **`orders-consumer`**: the Go service `orders-service`, a consumer group on `shop.orders` that commits offsets every second. The same image later runs against the target with only its connection variables changed.
- **`migrator`**: the `redpanda_migrator` input and output, authenticated as the `migrator` user with read-only ACLs on the source cluster and write ACLs on the target only for `shop.*`. The source Schema Registry has no authorization here, so the same user could write there.
- **`target`**: receives the topics with their configurations, every record with its timestamp and schema ID, every schema with its ID, and the translated offsets of `orders-service`. Its copy of `shop.orders` starts at offset 0, so the same record has a different offset on each cluster.
- **Redpanda Console**, one per cluster, signed in as the superuser.

### Data flow

Left to right: the producer looks up the ID of each topic's schema in the Confluent Schema Registry and writes Avro records to the four `shop.*` topics on Kafka; the `orders-service` group consumes `shop.orders` and commits offsets to `__consumer_offsets`.

Redpanda Migrator reads the topics through the Kafka API as the `migrator` user, reads the registry over HTTP with the same user, and periodically reads the committed offsets of every consumer group on those topics. On the target it creates each topic with the source's partition count and configuration, produces every record with its original key, headers, timestamp, and schema ID, plus two headers of its own (`redpanda-migrator-offset` with the source offset and `redpanda-migrator-provenance` with the source cluster's ID), registers every schema version under its original ID, and commits the translated offsets for `orders-service`. The target registry runs in `IMPORT` mode until the cutover so that every schema keeps its original ID.

At the cutover the consumer stops on the source, the migrator's next sync commits target offsets that point at the same records as the source's, and the same `orders-service` image starts on the target and continues from there, with no code change.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

A migration that cannot stop the business has three hard requirements. The applications must move without a rewrite. Every record must keep meaning the same thing, which for Avro means keeping its schema ID. And every consumer must resume at the record it would have read next, not at an offset number that means something else on the new cluster. Redpanda meets each of these:

- **Your clients move as they are.** Redpanda speaks the Kafka API and the Schema Registry API, so the shop's services, stock franz-go clients, keep their consumer groups, keyed partitioning, compaction, and Avro wire format, and the cutover changes `BROKERS` and `SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL` and nothing else. See [Kafka Compatibility](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/kafka-clients/).
- **Records, schemas, and consumer group offsets move in one pipeline.** Redpanda Migrator copies all three. MirrorMaker 2 copies records and offsets but not schemas, so a Kafka-to-Kafka migration usually runs a second tool for the registry. The migrator also adds the source offset to every copied record, which lets it translate the offset of a group with no active members (`Empty`) to the exact record even when offsets differ between the clusters. See [Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/).
- **Schema IDs survive.** The target's Schema Registry is part of the broker, and its `IMPORT` mode lets the migrator keep every schema ID, so records already on the wire decode on the target unchanged. See [Redpanda Schema Registry](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-overview/).
- **One tool on both sides.** The `rpk` CLI reads topics, consumer groups, ACLs, and schemas on Apache Kafka and Confluent Schema Registry as well as on Redpanda, so each inventory and comparison in this solution is the same command against either cluster. Only SCRAM user management on Kafka uses the Kafka CLI. See [rpk Commands](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/).

## Acceptance

The target is done when every rule holds and you can cite the evidence from the target itself: a configuration value, a code path, a test, or a measured result. The reference build's numbers do not transfer.

- [ ] Rule 1 holds (Start the environment).
- [ ] Rule 2 holds (Seed the source cluster).
- [ ] Rule 3 holds (Start the shop's workload).
- [ ] Rule 4 holds (Grant the migrator least-privilege access).
- [ ] Rule 5 holds (Start the migration).
- [ ] Rule 6 holds (Verify the schemas).
- [ ] Rule 7 holds (Monitor the migration lag).
- [ ] Rule 8 holds (Finish the cutover).
- [ ] Rule 9 holds (Verify end to end).
- [ ] Every Adapt item is answered, and any rule that does not apply to the target is recorded with the reason.

## Production gaps

This solution runs two single-node clusters with demo credentials so that it starts in a minute. Before you reuse the design for a real migration, work through each of these topics.

### Brokers and replication

In this solution, each cluster is one broker, so every topic has replication factor 1 on both sides, and the migrator copies the source's replication factor because nothing overrides it. The `max_in_flight` setting is 29, one batch per source partition, and `sync_topic_interval` creates a topic on the target even before it carries a record.

In production, run three or more brokers on the target and set `topic_replication_factor: 3` on the `redpanda_migrator` output, so migrated topics get the target's standard even when the source used less. Set `max_in_flight` to the number of partitions you migrate, and leave `sync_topic_interval` on so that empty and low-traffic topics are created too. Run the migrator close to the target cluster: it produces every record with acknowledgments, so produce latency to the target bounds its throughput.

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/) and [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/).

### Migrator throughput

In this solution, one migrator process copies about fifty records a second across 29 partitions, and its lag stays within a few seconds of production.

In production, measure before you commit to a cutover date:

- **What to measure.** The source's produce rate per topic in records and bytes, from your existing Kafka or MSK metrics. The migrator's copy rate and `redpanda_lag` per topic and partition while it copies history, and again once it is level with live traffic. The time the initial copy of retained history takes, which is the size of the retained data divided by the copy rate you measured.
- **Tuning one process.** The `redpanda_migrator` input and output document the settings for high throughput: `partition_buffer_bytes` and `max_yield_batch_bytes` on the input, and `max_in_flight` on the output, up to the number of partitions copied in parallel. Change one at a time and measure.
- **More than one process.** The input balances the source partitions across every process that shares its `consumer_group`, so you can run more migrator processes with the same configuration. Each process also runs the topic, schema, and consumer group syncs. Alternatively, split the topics between separate migrator processes, each with one input and output pair in its own config file and its own `regexp_topics_include` pattern and consumer group, so one team's large topics do not hold up another's. Test the layout you choose on a copy of your workload, including a restart of one process mid-copy.
- **Network cost and placement.** Every record crosses the network twice: read from the source and written to the target. When the clusters are in different availability zones, regions, or clouds, both legs can be billed as cross-zone or inter-region transfer, and the initial copy moves your whole retained history. Estimate it from the retained bytes plus the produce rate times the migration window, and place the migrator where it saves the most, usually in the same zone as the target, since its writes wait for acknowledgment.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/), [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/), and [Monitoring](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/guides/monitoring/).

### Security

In this solution, both clusters run SASL/SCRAM over plaintext listeners, the application and Console sign in as the superuser, and both Schema Registries sit behind HTTP basic auth. The Kafka node's controller listener is unauthenticated and bound to the loopback interface, which is why `ANONYMOUS` is in `super.users`. The `migrator` user has the least-privilege ACLs from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/) for the one group this solution migrates, `orders-service`.

In production, enable TLS on every Kafka listener and on Schema Registry, and give each application its own credential instead of the superuser. Secure a real Kafka source's controller listeners as its operators already do; never copy this demo's single-node controller setup. Reuse the migrator's ACL set with your topic prefix or an explicit topic list, plus `DESCRIBE` on the source and `READ` on the target for every consumer group you migrate: list the same groups in `consumer_groups.include`. With `DESCRIBE` on the cluster the migrator lists every group, including ones such as Confluent Schema Registry's `schema-registry` group, and a listed group it may not describe makes the offset fetch fail for the whole sync, with `GROUP_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED` in the migrator's log. Add `sync_topic_acls` and the cluster `ALTER` it needs on the target only if ACLs migrate too. Enable Schema Registry authorization so that the registry grants are as narrow as the Kafka ones, and rotate or delete the migrator's credential on both clusters once the last group has moved.

See [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/), [Configure Authentication](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authentication/), [Configure Access Control Lists](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/authorization/acl/), [Schema Registry Authorization](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-reg-authorization/), and the [migrator's required permissions](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/#required-permissions).

### Source authentication

In this solution, the migrator signs in to Apache Kafka with SASL/SCRAM-SHA-256 over plaintext and to Confluent Schema Registry with HTTP basic auth. That registry authenticates users from a file and authorizes nothing, so the migrator's registry user could write there.

In production, configure the `redpanda_migrator` input for your source:

- **Amazon MSK with IAM access control.** Set `sasl[].mechanism: AWS_MSK_IAM` with `sasl[].aws.region` and credentials (`from_ec2_role`, `role` to assume, or a `profile`), and turn on `tls`. Grant the IAM principal the same operations as the source ACLs in `scripts/migrator-acls.sh`, expressed as `kafka-cluster:` actions in an IAM policy: connect to and describe the cluster, read and describe the topics and their dynamic configuration, describe the groups you migrate, and describe and alter the migrator's own group. Amazon's IAM access control documentation maps each Kafka operation to its action; check the policy with the read-only proofs below.
- **Amazon MSK or Kafka with SCRAM.** Keep `SCRAM-SHA-512` or `SCRAM-SHA-256` as here, over TLS, and keep the ACLs in `scripts/migrator-acls.sh`.
- **OAUTHBEARER.** Set `sasl[].mechanism: OAUTHBEARER` with a `token`. The input sends that one token for each session and does not fetch a new one, so issue a token that outlives the migration window, or plan restarts with a fresh token, and test the behavior when it expires.
- **Confluent Schema Registry or Confluent Cloud.** The input's `schema_registry` block supports `basic_auth` (a Confluent Cloud API key and secret), `oauth`, `jwt`, and `tls` with client certificates. Give that identity read-only access to the subjects you migrate with the registry's own authorization, such as role bindings in Confluent Cloud or Confluent Platform, where it is available. Where it is not, as with the community registry here, treat the migrator's registry credential as a write credential and rotate it after the migration.

Whichever mechanism you use, run the read-only proofs from [Grant the migrator least-privilege access](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/grant-migrator-access/) against the real source before you start: listing topics works, and an idempotent produce and a `--acks 1` produce are both refused.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/) and the [migrator's required permissions](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/#required-permissions).

### Partitions

In this solution, the four topics have 12, 6, 8, and 3 partitions, and the migrator recreates each with the same count and copies every record to the same partition number.

In production, list every topic's partitions, configuration, and log start offsets with `rpk topic describe -c -p` and every subject with `rpk registry subject list` before you start; both work against Apache Kafka, Amazon MSK, and Confluent Schema Registry, so the final verification has a list to match. Keep partition counts identical during the migration: offset translation needs matching counts, and a different count on the target sends keys to other partitions. Resize on the target only after every consumer has moved. The migrator copies every topic setting on its supported list that the source reports, including Kafka's defaults such as `segment.bytes` and `max.message.bytes`, as topic-level overrides on the target, so compare `rpk topic describe -c` on both clusters and remove the overrides you want the target's cluster defaults for.

See [Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/manage-topics/).

### Schema validation

In this solution, schemas are registered on the source, the target registry stays in `IMPORT` mode until the cutover so that every ID is preserved, and no broker checks the schema ID of a record.

In production, freeze schema deletions on the source for the length of the migration, and keep `versions: all` so that consumers pinned to an old version keep working. Migrate in `IMPORT` mode with preserved IDs, return the target to `READWRITE` as the last step of the cutover, then enable schema ID validation on the migrated topics so that the target refuses a record whose schema it does not hold.

See [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/).

### Consumer scaling

In this solution, one consumer instance in `orders-service` moves by hand in [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/).

In production, list every group with `rpk group list` and `rpk group describe`, decide the order in which they move, and move each one with the same sequence: stop every instance on the source, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets, then start every instance on the target. Keep the migrator running until the last group and the last producer have moved.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Data retention

In this solution, the topics keep their source retention on the target: 7 days for `shop.orders`, compaction alone for `shop.customer-profiles`, 1 day with compaction for `shop.inventory-events`, and 1 hour for `shop.alerts`.

In production, check that the target's retention covers the migration window plus the backlog a consumer may still have at the cutover, and that the target has the disk for it.

See [Configure message retention](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/disk-utilization/#configure-message-retention).

### Compaction

In this solution, `shop.customer-profiles` is compacted and `shop.inventory-events` is compacted and deleted, but in a run this short compaction removes nothing before the migrator copies the records, so both topics hold the same number of records on the two clusters and `scripts/verify.sh` can compare the counts exactly.

In production, expect history that the source compacted before the migrator started: the source keeps the offset gaps that compaction left, and the migrator writes the remaining records one after another, so the target's high watermark for that topic is lower than the source's and the same record has different offsets. Compare compacted topics by key and latest value instead, and check each group's translated offsets by the records they point at (see [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery) for the gap case to test). Compaction runs on each cluster on its own schedule, so an older record for a key can still be on one side after it is gone from the other.

See [Compaction Settings](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/compaction-settings/).

### Cutover order

In this solution, the producer stops after the consumer has moved, the migrator drains, and `scripts/verify.sh` compares the two clusters once.

In production, create each application's user on the target and grant its ACLs there before you move it: the migrator copies no users, and copies topic ACLs only with `sync_topic_acls`, without their `WRITE` grants. Move every consumer group that reads a producer's topics before the producer, because until the producer moves, the source still has every record and each group can go back (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)). Then pause the producer, run the lag check until the migrator's lag on its topics is 0, and only then point it at the target. A producer that writes to the target before the drain finishes interleaves its records with migrated records that are still arriving, so records with the same key can land out of order. If a pause is not acceptable, accept that records produced to the target during the drain can precede migrated records with the same key. Run the comparisons in `scripts/verify.sh` as the acceptance test for each migrated topic and group, and keep the source cluster until they pass for the last one.

See [Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Rollback

In this solution, nothing is rolled back: the cutover runs forward once and `scripts/verify.sh` checks the result.

In production, plan the way back before each stage, and know which stage you are in:

- **Before any consumer moves.** The migrator only reads the source and writes the target. To abandon the migration, stop the migrator; the applications never noticed it. Delete the copied topics, schemas, and consumer groups on the target, or keep them for the next attempt.
- **After a consumer group moves, before its producers move.** The producers still write only to the source, so the source has every record and the group's committed offsets there have not moved since you stopped it. Stop the group's consumers on the target and start them on the source again with the source connection settings: they resume from the source offsets. Records the group processed on the target after the cutover are processed again, so this stage relies on the same idempotent processing as the cutover itself. The target's committed offsets for the group are now behind, and the migrator never moves a target offset backwards, so delete the group on the target (`rpk group delete`) before you try the cutover again.
- **After a producer writes to the target: the point of no return.** Records it writes exist only on the target, and the migrator copies in one direction. Going back means either copying those records to the source and then moving consumers back as above, or accepting that consumers on the source never see them. Every record the migrator copied carries its `redpanda-migrator-provenance` header and a record written to the target directly does not, so a Redpanda Connect pipeline from the target to the source can copy back only the records without that header. Build and test that pipeline before the cutover, because key order between copied-back records and the source's last records is yours to check. Decide which before you repoint the first producer, and repoint producers in the smallest groups you can, so that a rollback touches as few topics as possible.

Keep the source cluster, its consumer group offsets, and the migrator running until every group and producer has moved and `scripts/verify.sh` passes, so each earlier stage stays reversible for as long as possible.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/) and [rpk group delete](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-group/rpk-group-delete/).

### Migration runbook

In this solution, one person moves one consumer group and one producer in a few minutes.

In production, with dozens of topics and consumer groups owned by different teams, write the runbook before the migrator starts:

1. **Inventory.** List every topic with its partitions and configuration, every subject, every consumer group with its owner and the topics it reads, and every producer with the topics it writes. Note transactional producers and read_committed consumers (see [idempotency and delivery](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-idempotency-and-delivery)).
1. **Waves.** Group the topics so that each wave holds a set of producers and every consumer group that reads their topics. A group that reads topics of two waves moves with the later one. Give each wave an owner and a window.
1. **Gate: ready to copy.** Target sized and secured, migrator ACLs or IAM policy in place for the wave's topics and groups, the read-only proofs pass on the source, target registry in `IMPORT` mode.
1. **Gate: ready to move consumers.** Migration lag within the bound you set (`scripts/lag.sh --check` with your `LAG_BOUND`) for at least a full business cycle, no movement on any `redpanda_migrator_*_errors_total` counter, and the record and schema comparisons from `scripts/verify.sh` passing for the wave's topics.
1. **Move consumers, one group at a time.** For each group: stop it, wait until its target offsets point at the same records as its source offsets (`scripts/wait-for-offsets.sh`, adapted to the group), start it on the target, and check where it resumed (`scripts/resumed.sh`, adapted). No-go: any partition that resumed on another record. Rollback: move the group back to the source (see [rollback](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/verify-end-to-end/#prod-rollback)).
1. **Gate: ready to move producers, the point of no return.** Every consumer group of the wave runs on the target, stable and caught up, and each team has signed off. Pause the producers, drain to lag 0, repoint them.
1. **Close the wave.** Run the full comparison, keep the source topics read-only until the last wave is done, then retire them, leave `IMPORT` mode after the last wave, and delete the migrator's credentials.

See [Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/cookbooks/redpanda_migrator/) and [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Idempotency and delivery

In this solution, the source's `shop.orders` log starts after 1,200 trimmed records, so every copied record has a different offset on each cluster, and the consumer still resumes on the right record, which [Finish the cutover](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/finish-cutover/) and `scripts/verify.sh` check by comparing records, not offsets. No producer is transactional and no topic has been compacted yet.

In production, plan for how the migrator translates an offset. For each committed offset, it reads the record just before it on the source and finds the first target record with that timestamp or later. For a group in the `Empty` state, it then reads that record's `redpanda-migrator-offset` header, which holds the source offset, and moves to the exact record. For a group with active members, it stops at the timestamp lookup, which can land a few records early where several records on a partition share a millisecond timestamp, so a consumer that moves while its group is still active can read those records again. The migrator never moves a target offset backwards. So:

- Stop every consumer of a group before you wait for its offsets, so the group is `Empty` and its translation is exact, and keep consumers idempotent, or deduplicating by key, across the cutover anyway.
- Repoint a producer only after the migrator's lag on its topics is 0, so that no record written directly to the target precedes a migrated record with the same key.

Three source conditions need a test of their own before the cutover, on a copy of the real topics:

- **Transactional producers and read_committed consumers.** The input here uses `transaction_isolation_level: read_committed`, so it copies only committed records and skips aborted ones, and the target never sees the transaction markers. Each commit or abort marker on the source takes an offset that has no record on the target, so offsets drift further apart. A read_committed consumer usually commits an offset just after a commit marker, and the migrator reads the record just before the committed offset to translate it. Check what happens on your topics: watch `redpanda_migrator_cg_offset_translation_errors_total` for each group, compare the records the source and target offsets point at with `scripts/compare-offsets.sh`, and move a test group before a real one. The output has no transactional setting and writes copied records outside any transaction, so a read_committed consumer on the target reads every copied record.
- **Trimmed log starts.** Retention or `DeleteRecords` moves the source's log start offset, as here. The migrator copies from the log start, so the target starts at 0. A group whose committed offset is at or below the source's log start offset is skipped (there is no earlier record to translate from), and a consumer of that group starts on the target from its `auto.offset.reset` policy. Find such groups with `rpk group describe` before the cutover.
- **Compaction gaps.** A compacted source topic has offsets with no record, and the target copy has none, so offsets differ there too. If the record just before a committed offset was compacted away, the migrator cannot read it to translate that offset. Count the translation errors per group, and compare the record each offset points at rather than the offset numbers.

See [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/outputs/redpanda_migrator/) and [redpanda_migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/components/inputs/redpanda_migrator/).

### Dead-letter handling

In this solution, there is no dead-letter topic: a record the migrator cannot write is retried, and the pipeline stops on a permanent error.

In production, keep that behavior, since a migration that drops records is not a migration. Alert on `output_error` and on a rising `redpanda_lag`, fix the cause (usually a missing ACL or a full disk on the target), and keep the source until the target has been verified.

See [Error Handling](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/configuration/error_handling/).

### Observability

In this solution, `make lag` reads the migrator's Prometheus endpoint, and each cluster has its own Redpanda Console.

In production, scrape the migrator's `/metrics` (`redpanda_lag` and the `redpanda_migrator_*` counters) and both clusters into your monitoring. Alert when lag stays above a bound you set, the produce rate times the delay you accept, as `scripts/lag.sh --check` does with `LAG_BOUND`, and when any `redpanda_migrator_*_errors_total` counter moves, including `redpanda_migrator_cg_offset_translation_errors_total`.

See [Monitoring](https://docs.redpanda.com/connect/guides/monitoring/) and [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/).

### Disaster recovery

In this solution, there is no standby: the source is the only other copy, and it is retired after the cutover.

In production, set up Shadowing after the migration so that a second Redpanda cluster stays level with the target, including consumer group offsets and schemas, and can take over if the target fails. The disaster recovery solution, [Survive a cluster outage without reconfiguring clients](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/), builds that setup end to end.

See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

In this solution, nothing reads the migrated topics except `orders-service`.

In production, enable Iceberg topics on the migrated topics that analytics needs, so the brokers write each record to an Iceberg table with no extra pipeline to run.

See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).

## The problem

A shop writes every confirmed order to one topic, and a fulfillment consumer group ships from it. If that cluster goes away, two numbers decide the damage: orders lost (the recovery point) and how long fulfillment stops (the recovery time).

You build two Redpanda clusters joined by a shadow link, behind one Envoy address. You kill the primary under a live workload, fail over, and measure both numbers: the lost records, and the seconds until reads and writes resume.

## What the system must do

- Configure one shadow link that replicates a topic's records and a consumer group's committed offsets to a second cluster
- Prove parity partition by partition before you trust the link with a failover
- Route Kafka clients through Envoy so that a failover needs no change to the client's configuration
- Kill the primary under a running producer and consumer, and count the acknowledged records the failover lost and the records each consumer group processes again
- Fail shadow topics over, report the recovery times, and show that a consumer resumes from the replicated offsets instead of reprocessing the topic

The stack runs on Docker Compose or on Kubernetes, where the two clusters and the link are `Redpanda` and `ShadowLink` resources for the Redpanda Operator. [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/start-environment/) has a tab for each.

## Rules

Every rule must hold in the target system.

1. Run the recovery target as a separate, independently deployed cluster, and put the client-routing proxy in front of both clusters from the first day, not during the incident. (from [Start the environment](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/start-environment/))
2. Replicate consumer group offsets along with the records, scope the link's topic and group filters to a named prefix instead of `*`, and start a new link at the earliest offset. (from [Create the shadow link](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/create-shadow-link/))
3. Prove replication parity before you need it by comparing both clusters' high watermarks partition by partition, check replicated consumer offsets separately, and treat the replication lag just before a failure as your recovery point. (from [Produce and consume the orders through Envoy, then prove parity](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/route-clients-through-envoy/))
4. Rehearse the outage as an ungraceful kill under live writes and commits, let the proxy move clients for reads automatically, keep shadow topics read-only until a person promotes them, and decide in advance what happens to the writes refused in that window. (from [Simulate the disaster](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/simulate-disaster/))
5. Keep promotion a separate, manual, irreversible step from the client move, taken only once someone decides the source cluster is gone for good, and time it in every rehearsal. (from [Fail the shadow topics over](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/fail-over/))
6. Record each claim at the moment you measure it, because parity before an outage cannot be measured after it, and verify a recovery with exact equalities on watermarks, committed offsets, and topic state in a scheduled rehearsal. (from [Verify the recovery end to end](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/))

## System map

The reference system, to map against what the target already has.

Two single-broker Redpanda clusters with Shadowing enabled, one shadow link between them, and an Envoy proxy in front of both. A Python client plays the shop: it produces orders and reads them as the fulfillment consumer group, through Envoy, and it is never told that there are two clusters. You kill the source cluster while a second workload is still writing and committing, and the client reads every replicated record through the same address once Envoy moves it.

- **Source cluster** (`redpanda-source`): the cluster that serves clients until it fails.
- **Shadow cluster** (`redpanda-shadow`): the failover target. It runs the link, fetches from the source, and holds the replicated topics read-only until you promote them.
- **The shadow link `disaster-recovery`**: one configuration file that replicates every topic whose name starts with `dr-`, with its records (`topic_metadata_sync_options`), and the committed offsets of every consumer group whose ID starts with `dr-` (`consumer_offset_sync_options`).
- **Envoy**: the only Kafka endpoint clients are given, a TCP proxy that does not parse Kafka. Each cluster has a listener that advertises its broker as `envoy:9092`, so the metadata a client gets back always points it at Envoy, whichever cluster answered. Envoy health checks each cluster with a Kafka request and sends traffic to the source cluster while it answers and to the shadow cluster when it does not.
- **Python client**, built on kafka-python 2.3.2: the order-capture service and the fulfillment consumer. It produces 12 orders to `dr-orders`, reads them as the `dr-consumers` group, reads them again during the outage as a separate group that the link does not replicate, and resumes as `dr-consumers` after the failover to read only the new records. One bootstrap address throughout.
- **A live workload**, `scripts/stream.py` in the same client: a producer that writes `dr-order-events` 20 times a second and records every acknowledged offset, a consumer group that commits after every batch, and a sampler that reads both clusters' watermarks once a second. It runs while the source is killed, so the recovery point is counted rather than assumed.
- **Two Redpanda Consoles**, one per cluster: the source view is what you lose in the outage, and the shadow view is where you watch replication arrive.
- **Kubernetes manifests**: the same two clusters and the same link as `Redpanda` and `ShadowLink` resources for the Redpanda Operator, and every other service as a Deployment of the same name, for the Kubernetes path.

### Data flow

Left to right: the client holds one address, `envoy:9092`. Envoy forwards the connection, byte for byte, to the source cluster, its priority 0 endpoint. The source answers on a listener that advertises its broker as `envoy:9092`, so the client's next connection comes back to Envoy instead of going straight to a broker. Behind the clusters, the shadow link runs on the shadow cluster and pulls from the source. Its topic sync task creates a shadow topic for every source topic that matches the `dr-` filter and replicates its records from the first offset. Its consumer offset sync task copies the committed offsets of every group that matches the same prefix. While the link is active, the shadow topics reject writes.

When the source cluster stops answering, Envoy's health check fails and it moves traffic to its priority 1 endpoint, the shadow cluster, whose listener advertises the same `envoy:9092`. Reads resume on the same address as soon as the health checks fail the source, because the replicated records are already there; [Fail the shadow topics over](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/fail-over/) reports how long that took in your run, and how many acknowledged records the link had not copied yet. Writes are still refused, because a shadow topic is read-only by design: that is what stops both clusters accepting writes at once. The `rpk shadow failover` command promotes the shadow topics to ordinary topics, and from that point the same address serves reads and writes from the shadow cluster, with each consumer group resuming from the offset the link replicated.

### Platform capabilities the design depends on

A disaster recovery setup is only as good as its failover. A second cluster has to stay current without anyone watching it. Consumers have to resume where they left off, not reprocess the day or skip records. Nothing may write to the standby while the primary is still alive, or the two diverge. And the whole arrangement has to be simple enough to rehearse, because a failover nobody has practiced is a guess. Redpanda builds this into the broker with Shadowing:

- **One link for records and consumer offsets, in the broker.** Shadowing replicates the topics and the consumer group offsets from one configuration file, with no connector, no separate replication cluster, and no state store to operate: the destination cluster fetches from the source and reports its own lag. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).
- **Offsets preserved.** A shadow topic keeps the source's offsets, so an offset a consumer committed on the source means the same record on the shadow, and a replicated commit needs no translation. See [Shadowing Overview](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/overview/).
- **Read-only until you promote.** Shadow topics reject produce requests until you fail them over, so a proxy that moves clients early cannot cause a split brain, and the promotion is a separate, auditable step a person takes. See [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/).
- **The same link on Kubernetes.** The Redpanda Operator takes the link as a `ShadowLink` resource, so the recovery topology is part of the cluster's desired state. See [cluster.redpanda.com/v1alpha2](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/k-crd/).

Because the clients speak the Kafka API, they need no Redpanda-specific failover logic: the stock kafka-python clients here reconnect through Envoy, a TCP proxy that health-checks both clusters, to whichever one is serving, and resume from their group's committed offsets as on any Kafka cluster. If you run Kafka or Amazon MSK today, [Migrate from Kafka to Redpanda with Redpanda Migrator](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/kafka-migration/) moves a live workload's topics, schemas, and consumer group offsets to Redpanda first.

## Production gaps

This solution runs one broker on each side with no authentication, and a proxy with one endpoint per cluster, so that it starts in a minute. Before you build a recovery plan on the design, work through each topic below.

### Brokers and replication

In this solution, each cluster is one broker in `dev-container` mode with replication factor 1, and the link copies the source topic's `replication.factor` onto the shadow topic.

In production, run three or more brokers per cluster with replication factor 3, in separate failure domains, and give the shadow cluster the capacity to take the source's full load on the day it is promoted. More brokers also change the proxy: each one needs its own advertised address (see [client routing](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-client-routing)).

See [Deploy for Production: Manual](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/production/production-deployment/) and [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/).

### Security

In this solution, everything is plaintext: the link connects to the source without TLS or credentials, and neither cluster authenticates clients or the proxy.

In production, enable TLS and SASL on both clusters, scope the link's credentials to reading the topics and groups it replicates, encrypt the connection between clients and Envoy, and set `security_sync_options` on the link so that ACLs arrive on the shadow cluster with the data.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Configure Kafka TLS Encryption](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/encryption/).

### Client routing

In this solution, one Envoy container forwards one listener to one broker per cluster. Envoy does not parse Kafka; each cluster's `proxied` listener advertises its broker as `envoy:9092`, so any Kafka client is sent back to Envoy whichever cluster answers. It is tested with kafka-python 2.3.2. Envoy health checks each cluster with a Kafka ApiVersions request on that listener, which proves the listener accepts a connection and answers a Kafka request, but not that partitions have leaders or that writes succeed. A plain TCP check would pass on a listener that accepts connections and never answers, and the Admin API's `/v1/status/ready` answers on a different listener, so it can pass while the Kafka listener is wedged.

In production, a Kafka client connects to each partition's leader, so the proxy needs one address per broker, and the shape is:

- One proxy listener, and one Envoy cluster holding a source and shadow endpoint pair at priorities 0 and 1, per broker id. Broker N of each Redpanda cluster advertises the same proxy address for its listener, for example `envoy.example.internal:9092+N`, so the two Redpanda clusters need the same number of brokers and the same broker ids.
- All listeners fail over together. A single source broker failing is an event the source cluster survives by moving leadership; if only that broker's listener moved, one client would talk to both clusters at once. Health check every source endpoint against one shared address that answers while any source broker does (a load balancer in front of the source's client listeners), so the listeners move only when the whole cluster stops answering. The file `envoy/envoy-three-brokers.yaml` is an example of this for three brokers; this solution does not run it.
- The proxy is not a single point of failure. Run two or more Envoy instances with the same configuration behind a TCP load balancer or a DNS name. They make their health decisions independently and can disagree for a few seconds during an outage; that is safe for writes only because shadow topics refuse them until the promotion.

Without a proxy, give clients a DNS name or load balancer per broker and switch it at failover in the runbook. Envoy's Kafka broker filter can rewrite broker addresses in Metadata responses instead of relying on advertised listeners, but it decodes only the request versions it was built with and closes connections it cannot decode, so test your client's negotiated versions against it.

Envoy's priority list is symmetric: it sends clients back to the source as soon as the source passes its health checks again. Make the proxy change part of the failover runbook and do it before the old primary restarts, as the failback extension does with `envoy/envoy-promoted.yaml`. Shadowing has no automatic fallback, and the proxy must not add one.

See [Configure Listeners](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/security/listener-configuration/), [Failover](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover/), and [Failover Runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/).

### Partitions

In this solution, one topic has three partitions, and the link copies the source partition count onto the shadow topic.

In production, size the partitions on the source. Adding partitions to a source topic after the link exists adds them to the shadow topic too, and every consumer group has to cope with the change on both clusters.

See [Sizing Guidelines](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/manual/sizing/).

### Schema validation

In this solution, the orders are plain JSON with no schema ID, so the link does not replicate the Schema Registry and neither broker validates records.

In production, add `schema_registry_sync_options` to the link: topic mode (`shadow_schema_registry_topic`) for a Redpanda source, API mode for a Confluent-compatible registry. After a failover, enable schema ID validation on the promoted topics so that a producer pointed at the new primary cannot write records the consumers cannot decode.

See [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/) and [Server-Side Schema ID Validation](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/schema-reg/schema-id-validation/).

### Consumer scaling

In this solution, one consumer instance in the `dr-consumers` group reads three partitions.

In production, scale each group on its lag, and size the shadow cluster for every group reconnecting and catching up at the same moment, not for the steady state.

See [Consumer Offsets](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/consume-data/consumer-offsets/).

### Data retention

In this solution, the link starts at the earliest offset and syncs `retention.ms` and `segment.ms` from the source.

In production, keep the retention properties in the link's synced properties so the shadow topics match the source, and use Tiered Storage on the shadow cluster to make long retention affordable.

See [Use Tiered Storage](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/tiered-storage/).

### Compaction

In this solution, `dr-orders` uses the default delete policy, and the link syncs `cleanup.policy` along with the compaction properties, as the Synced Shadow Topic Properties list in `rpk shadow status` shows.

In production, check that every compacted topic in the link's filters keeps its `cleanup.policy` and compaction lag settings on the shadow cluster, because a consumer that rebuilds state from a compacted topic after a failover reads whatever the shadow cluster kept.

See [Compaction Settings](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/cluster-maintenance/compaction-settings/).

### Idempotency and delivery

In this solution, the client produces with `acks=all` and no retries, so a failed write is visible rather than silently duplicated.

In production, enable idempotence and document the cut-over order. A producer that writes to both clusters during a failover produces records that no replication can reconcile.

See [Idempotent producers](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/produce-data/idempotent-producers/).

### Dead-letter handling

In this solution, nothing handles them. A write that the shadow topic refuses surfaces as a `PolicyViolationError` in the client, and the streaming producer only records each one in `state/stream-errors.jsonl`.

In production, buffer the producer's writes or send them to a dead-letter store during the window between the outage and the failover, and replay them once the promoted topics accept writes. Rehearse that window: it is the part of the plan that only shows up in an incident.

See [Failover Runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/) and [Configure Producers](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/develop/produce-data/configure-producers/).

### Observability

In this solution, you read `rpk shadow status`, `make parity`, `make offsets`, and Envoy's admin API by hand.

In production, alert on the link's lag and task states (the [recovery point and recovery time](https://docs.redpanda.com/solutions/disaster-recovery/verify-end-to-end/#prod-recovery-point-and-time) topic lists the metrics), on Envoy's endpoint health and priority changes, and on the difference between the two clusters' high watermarks. A link whose lag grew unnoticed is not a recovery plan.

See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/) and [Monitor Redpanda](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/monitoring/).

### Disaster recovery

In this solution, one link fails over once, in one direction, and the walkthrough stops there. The failback extension on the last step reverses it.

In production, follow the failover runbook, including the decision to fail over, who makes it, and the client cut-over. Plan the failback as its own operation, because a failover cannot be undone and the old primary's log diverged at the moment it failed:

1. Change the proxy, DNS, or load balancer so that clients prefer the promoted cluster, before the old primary starts again.
1. Rebuild the old primary empty, with topic auto-creation off, so that no client creates a topic there before the reverse link creates its shadow topic. Records it wrote after the last replicated offset exist nowhere else; recover them from the producers or accept their loss, but do not bring them back in place.
1. Delete the original link with `rpk shadow delete` once its topics are `FAILED_OVER`, and create a reverse link on the old primary that fetches from the promoted cluster, with the same filters and `start_at_earliest`.
1. Wait for parity on every partition and for the consumer group offsets, and keep watching the reverse link's lag until the window. A link that has not read the source yet reports no lag or `-1`, not 0, so do not read either as caught up.
1. In a maintenance window, stop the producers, check parity again and stop if it fails, switch the proxy back to the old primary while its topics are still read-only, run `rpk shadow failover` on the reverse link, and restart the producers.
1. Rebuild the other cluster empty and recreate the original link, so the primary is protected again.

Review the link's topic, group, and security filters whenever the recovery plan changes, and keep the link configuration and the cluster manifests in Git so that the recovery topology is reviewed like any other change. On Kubernetes, put the two clusters in two Kubernetes clusters in separate regions. Run this solution's verification as a scheduled rehearsal against a real pair of clusters, kill the primary rather than stopping it, and give the report to someone who reads it.

See [Failover Runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/), [rpk shadow delete](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/reference/rpk/rpk-shadow/rpk-shadow-delete/), [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/), and [Deploy Redpanda for Production in Kubernetes](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/deploy/redpanda/kubernetes/k-production-deployment/).

### Recovery point and recovery time

In this solution, both clusters run on one machine, so the round trip between them is well under a millisecond. The `make recovery-report` target counts the acknowledged records a kill lost, the replication lag in the last sample before it, how far each streaming consumer group falls back, and the recovery times on that machine, with no decision time.

In production, treat the replication lag at the moment of failure as your recovery point, because Shadowing replicates asynchronously, and expect it to be larger across regions. Three things set a floor under it that no amount of capacity removes:

- The round trip between the regions. Every fetch the shadow cluster makes costs at least one, so records written within the last round trip are always at risk.
- The fetch wait. The link's fetcher waits up to `fetch_wait_max_ms` (500 ms by default) for `fetch_min_bytes` to accumulate, so at low throughput the shadow trails by up to that wait plus the round trip. Lower it for a tighter floor, at the cost of more fetch requests.
- The consumer offset sync interval. Committed offsets travel every `interval` under `consumer_offset_sync_options`, so a group can lose up to that interval of commits and reprocess those records after a failover, on top of the records lost from the topic.

Cross-region replication also costs egress: the source region pays for every byte the shadow cluster fetches, which `redpanda_shadow_link_total_bytes_fetched` measures. Size the link's scope with its filters for that bill.

Monitor these Shadowing metrics, and alert on:

- The lag metric, `redpanda_shadow_link_shadow_lag`, per `shadow_link_name`, `topic`, and `partition`: when it exceeds the records your RPO allows (your write rate times the seconds of data you can lose), or keeps growing without recovering.
- Client errors, `redpanda_shadow_link_client_errors`: when it rises quickly, which means the shadow cluster is struggling to reach the source.
- Topic states, `redpanda_shadow_link_shadow_topic_state` per `state`: when any topic is in `FAULTED`.
- Throughput, `redpanda_shadow_link_total_records_fetched` and `redpanda_shadow_link_total_bytes_fetched`: when they drop sharply while the source is still taking writes.
- The link's task states in `rpk shadow status`: when a task reports `FAULTED`, `NOT_RUNNING`, or `LINK_UNAVAILABLE`.

Record the recovery time for reads and for writes in each rehearsal, as the runbook asks; the time to decide usually dominates the write time.

See [Monitor Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/monitor/), [Configure Shadowing](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/setup/), and [Failover Runbook](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/disaster-recovery/shadowing/failover-runbook/).

### Analytics and lakehouse

In this solution, there is no analytics path.

In production, a shadow cluster is also a place to read the replicated data without loading the primary: Iceberg topics on the shadow cluster write it to a lakehouse table.

See [About Iceberg Topics](https://docs.redpanda.com/streaming/current/manage/iceberg/about-iceberg-topics/).
